We introduce a new type of logistic model delayed by $\tau > 0$ and include the parameter $0 \leqslant \gamma \leqslant 1$ to weigh between current and past population levels. A logarithmically delayed term reflects how biological populations react slowly, as the delayed feedback in growth responses can cause oscillations. We examine the existence and positivity of solutions, along with zero solutions and equilibrium points. We prove that a unique positive solution exists and is global, ensuring that solutions remain positive over time given non-negative and non-trivial initial conditions. We further establish that solutions starting within our defined class of initial functions converge to a single positive steady state. Finally, linking our findings to a cell-biological mechanism, we demonstrate that global attractivity arises when the feedback mechanism acts exclusively on past population levels and demonstrate that delays have little impact when the $\gamma$ parameter significantly reduces the delayed feedback influence.

Statistical depth offers an effective method for characterizing the centrality of multivariate point observations relative to an entire dataset. Recent research has introduced the rMAD (rotated Mahalanobis) depth framework for points, which was extended in the present study to incorporate Depth Contour Maps (DCMs) and a new metric called rMAD depth. However, this prior work limited its scope to datasets free of zeros and exhibited reduced robustness. The present paper introduces a novel three-stage approach for constructing the rMAD depth of positive data through robust partial log-transformation (log-p), specifically targeting ratios. Consequently, this new methodology successfully extends statistical depth metrics to positive datasets. An illustrative example using UK small business financial data validates the utility of this approach. Finally, a computational package named `rmad_depth` has been released on CRAN, featuring functions for calculating rMAD depth, generating depth-contour maps, and applying the new log-p based methodology.

We propose an idealized superconducting hybrid system designed to investigate the dynamics of coupled electronic and photonic degrees of freedom at a circuit level. This model, which integrates circuit quantization with quantum electrodynamics, extends the standard input-output formalism to a fully quantum framework. Crucially, this formulation assumes that all components possess circuit parameters that are significantly smaller than their respective environmental coupling rates, enabling the significant simplification of otherwise intricate equations. Consequently, the resulting formalism provides a foundational basis for substantially reduced descriptive models of various superconducting hybrid devices.

This study introduces a new technique for accurately determining nuclear masses by combining a Penning trap with an ion cyclotron resonance (ICR) spectrometer. The precision of the resulting mass-to-charge ratio ($A/q$) depends on the system's $B\rho$ value—the product of magnetic field strength ($B$) and the radius ($\rho$) of the curved path followed by the moving ion. The measurement methodology involves synchronizing the system's timing with the time required for an ion to traverse a specific, pre-calibrated isochronous path within the same device. By comparing the system's actual ICR period against this defined $B\rho$-based period, the necessary parameters for calculating the final mass are derived. The validity of this approach was validated through measurements of the $A/q=1$ for the $^{12}$C and $A/q=1$ for the $^{208}$Pb isotopes, as well as by analyzing the $A/q=1$ for the $^{100}$Sn nucleus. These validation runs confirmed the method's exceptional accuracy, yielding relative mass measurement uncertainties of $1.2\times 10^{-9}$ for $^{12}$C and $1.7\times 10^{-9}$ for $^{208}$Pb.

We examine extension flows that connect lattice regularized approaches to continuum models, emphasizing real-field systems where Monte Carlo simulations are viable. A key advantage of extension flows is their capacity to efficiently integrate fermionic degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we examine how to combine these standardizing flows with the "fermionization at will" technique to clear detritonons in the acceptance ratio of the Metropolis algorithm.

Recently, Deep Learning (DL) has excelled in handling many image recognition tasks; however, it struggles to reliably identify algorithms and tools for computer programming. This limitation arises because DL models typically lack the ability to understand or anticipate a program's structural patterns. While previous studies attempted to address this by creating image input structures that favored specific syntax rules (such as parentheses matching), these approaches failed to cover the full range of structural patterns found in real-world code.

In this paper, we introduce a new method to generate structured text images designed for programming. Our approach extends beyond common patterns to validate a broader spectrum of rules, specifically by incorporating Regular Expressions. We evaluate this technique using two standard benchmarks for Code Image-to-Text tasks: one focused on image identification language and another for Scala code identification. Results demonstrate that structuring the images improves the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Most critically, our structure is effective enough to enable the Vision Transformer architecture to outperform CNNs on these recognition tasks, successfully completing this "victory swap" of model architectures.

This study explores the potential for creating top quark pairs in proton-nucleus ($p$A$) collisions via high-energy lepton–positron colliders, specifically targeting future machines like CLIC or ILC. The work examines the top-antiquark ($t\bar{t}$) yield as a function of both integrated luminosity and the nuclear target material (specifically deuterium and silicon) across a $ \sqrt{s} $ range from 300 GeV to 10 TeV. Utilizing PYTHIA 8.210 with LHC 2.10 to simulate hadronic processes and LEPTOP to model the $ t\bar t $ production cross section within a lepton collider framework, the authors calculate cross sections alongside the transverse momentum ($ p_{\mathrm{T}} $) spectra for the resulting quarks. Results are presented using dimensionless ratios normalized against proton-nucleus ($pA$) collisions and pure proton-proton ($pp$) collisions to assess nuclear effects on elementary quark pair production mechanisms.

This study introduces an auxiliary task-oriented, end-to-end framework for natural language query generation across different domains, extending and refining the blue-style model proposed by Devlin et al. (2012). We observe that existing approaches struggle with knowledge transfer due to domain-specific schema variations. To resolve this, we leverage a schema-independent generation task as a bridge to facilitate cross-domain learning, effectively transferring semantic understanding from a source domain to a target domain with novel schemas. For the semantic component, we train a dedicated encoder on a source domain to generate intermediate representations of natural language inputs; these semantic vectors are then integrated with newly structured database schemas to encode context for the target domain. Finally, the blue-style architecture applies this combined encoding to produce SQL statements. We evaluated the framework using two distinct text-to-SQL datasets as separate cases and compared its performance against leading existing methods. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy.

The radio emission from star-forming galaxies primarily stems from non-thermal processes involving active nuclear black holes or non-thermal bursts within Galactic histories. Using first data from the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey, we examined the connection between galaxy redshift and radio luminosity across four frequency bands (425–525 MHz to 625–725 MHz), analyzing over 100,000 sources with luminosity exceeding $10^{21} \text{ W Hz}^{-1} \text{ at } 150 \text{ MHz}$. Our findings confirm that redshift distribution shifts toward higher values as radio luminosity grows, a trend observable in all studied frequencies. However, this trend weakens at frequencies above 600 MHz; consequently, we calculated an optimal frequency band for studying the galaxy-radio luminosity relationship. Furthermore, we assessed biasing factors by comparing the radio correlation function with that of the galaxy count, finding no significant difference between them. This lack of disparity implies that the radio survey does not heavily miss out on missing blue galaxies.

The high-dimensional ranking Lasso is a widely used technique for establishing preferences among multiple alternatives across diverse domains. Although the method proves effective in scenarios with a vast number of rankings limited to low dimensions, its utility is hindered in problems involving moderately large dimensions constrained by low rank counts. This paper introduces a novel approach that integrates a global adaptive step-size strategy with a new screening rule, resulting in a highly efficient algorithm capable of handling high-dimensional spaces with many categories. theoretical results confirm the validity of our proposed screening rule, while numerical evaluations demonstrate that the resulting solutions yield substantial performance gains on real-world datasets.

A thermodynamic process is considered entropy generating when its average value across all possible realizations is strictly positive. This paper establishes that, for a broad category of quantum channels, the minimum entropy production within the ensemble is convex relative to the ensemble's probability distribution. This property holds true regardless of whether the processes involved are reversible at the limit of zero probability of irreversibility. Notably, this convexity property enables the derivation of a lower bound on entropy production for any arbitrary ensemble of rapid nonequilibrium processes, a feature potentially pivotal in advancing quantum energy harvesting and the theory of fluctuating quantum engines.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a pivotal force in combating climate change and addressing ecological challenges, yet its inherent carbon footprint is frequently overlooked. This study aims to quantify the environmental benefits AI confers to society versus the negative environmental harm it causes, while also assessing the net impact of its deployment. Furthermore, it seeks to uncover the inherent characteristics of AI models that result in negative environmental outcomes and to contrast these findings across different execution platforms. To achieve this, we established an evaluation framework that integrates machine learning model training with physical resource usage metrics. Utilizing state-of-the-art solutions, including an AI-powered environmental assessment system, we evaluated the characteristics of deep neural network models. By integrating carbon emission data with equivalent full-time employee hours, we determined that these AI systems generate more ecological benefits than harms. However, our analysis reveals that certain negative environmental impacts are concealed within AI workflows and are inextricably linked to specific model features, indicating that not all models are inherently eco-friendly. Additionally, while these adverse effects are minimal when assessed in terms of employee hours, the variation in environmental performance across different deployment platforms suggests that selecting an AI model requires careful consideration of both functional efficacy and environmental suitability.

Prescriptive process monitoring focuses on the monitoring phase of a prescriptive monitoring system. In such a system, monitoring mechanisms not only identify and explain ongoing process deviations but also suggest actions to stakeholders to further development of an optimal path. These suggestions are formulated based on the observation of the system's past and current states alongside a prior knowledge of its dynamics. The primary objective of this work is to analyze the academic landscape of the historical development of these systems. Specifically, it examines the evolution of the methods and algorithms employed for the monitoring phase. Additionally, it outlines the most promising research directions for the systems.

To manage thermal processes, we develop a novel A Posteriori error management (APARM) strategy based on a generalized Boussinesq model within a Lagrangian framework. The design of this approach is driven by two primary objectives: first, minimizing temperature fluctuations in the fluid to enhance reaction uniformity for substances being heated or cooled; second, reducing the physical space occupied by the reacting substance to save material volume. This architecture represents the inaugural application of APARM in reaction-advection-diffusion contexts, where it simultaneously addresses temperature stability and volume efficiency. The proposed method proves versatile for a diverse range of technologies, including exothermic reactions, chemical processes, and systems governed by a generalized Boussinesq model. The core concept involves calculating APARM across the entire domain to identify two critical outputs derived from an error-based feedback loop. The first utilizes a domain-wide temperature variance metric to determine localized heating or cooling adjustments; specifically, if variance is high, additional energy input is required, whereas low variance indicates sufficient temperature stability. The second maps a functional relationship between density and spatial coordinates; by evaluating desired density levels for each location, this method identifies regions needing expansion or contraction. These functions are then executed to regulate both thermal uniformity and volumetric reaction outcomes. The efficacy of this strategy is validated through numerical simulations on a generalized Boussinesq model, with performance assessed using specific APARM indicators. The study further demonstrates the method's robustness by testing it under uncertain initial and boundary conditions

Kernelization serves as a method to resolve the "curse of dimensionality," enabling efficient distance-based modeling within high-dimensional spaces. The standard kernel function computes distances in this space by measuring the distance between projected points. However, when the mean distance in high dimensions is typically near $\sqrt{m}$ (where $m$ represents $m$-dimensional features), small variations in low dimensions can cause large relative errors due to this convergence to a constant value, deucing model accuracy relying on precise distance calculations. To mitigate these risks, we introduce two novel kernelizers designed to preserve the original low-dimensional distance distributions rather than solely focusing on constant convergence. The first approach estimates and removes distances by regressing them against $\ell_1$ norms of their components. The second approach models the distance as a Gaussian distribution conditioned on $\ell_1$ norm and samples from this distribution instead. We evaluate these new frameworks over two datasets using both metric learning and one-class classification tasks, comparing them against conventional kernels, a linear transformation to the high-dimensional domain, and alternatives that do not require such dimensionality conversion.

In this work, we examine how agents' opinions evolve alongside their confidence levels in response to information environments characterized by a "preferential shift." This shift occurs when agents consistently favor inaccurate information over accurate information during learning interactions. Utilizing a dynamic framework that links the learning process with an agent's uncertainty, our findings indicate that, as opinion evolution reaches a stable equilibrium, a significant portion of the population adopts extreme positions. Crucially, the fraction holding these radical views includes not only agents initially biased toward extreme information but also those who lack initial bias or confidence limitations. Notably, the final distribution is highly sensitive to the proportion of agents holding initially extreme positions. Furthermore, the observed outcomes provide empirical support for real-world observations: the emergence of polarized public discourse often coincides with an abundance of misleading information circulating within society.

Black objects that support hair cannot be fully characterized by their mass, charge, and angular momentum alone; an additional set of observables is required. We posit that at large distances, the spatial profile of this hair is the most relevant additional descriptor. When this profile remains smooth and decays rapidly at the level we describe, it is called "asymptotic," meaning it can be rendered by a finite collection of parameters that define its shape, scale, and specific function. We examine hairy black stars (BBS) within Einstein-Aborn-Router theory to see if this concept applies. Our analysis indicates that BBS objects can display hair at every scale rather than just asymptotically, as they possess both a massive scale and an asymptotic one. We present the BBS's interior structure, finding a quasicontinuum of such stars bounded by a singular star. Notably, this quasicontinuum arises because a parameter is quantized, allowing for an infinite set of solutions. We further explore stability issues, energy radiation, entropy, and potential experimental verification methods.

Although cells convert genetic information into transcripts to regulate protein synthesis, the specific conditions governing this transcriptional production remain poorly understood. We address this gap by constructing a genome-wide probabilistic model of transcript generation based on the temporal patterns of nascent RNA labeled with different tags in human cells. By fitting this model to data derived from genomic sites containing poly-A sequences, we observed that transcription initiation typically spans 10 to 20 minutes before the synthesis of the initial mRNA molecule. Furthermore, we noted variations in the lag duration correlated with promoter characteristics, including features enabling rapid activation and efficient termination by the ribonucleotide reductase complex enzyme. Finally, our results indicate that transcriptional output lag correlates with overall transcriptional strength, suggesting an inherent property inherent to cellular machinery that potentially buffers cellular systems against fluctuations in initiation rates.

A standard result in coding theory establishes that for a code $C$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ with dual $C^\perp$, $C$ is equivalent to a linear complement of its orthogonal complement if the sum of their dimensions equals the code length, i.e., $\dim(C) + \dim(C^\perp) = n$. Extending this concept, we define the Linear Complementarity Property (LCP) within modules over the finite principal ideal ring $R = \mathbb{F}_{q^m}[x]/(x^2)$. Consequently, this study investigates the structure of $R$-linear codes and provides the permutation equivalent definition of the LCP. We further examine the relationship between the LCP and that of the underlying projective space $P^{m-1}(\mathbb{F}_{q^m})$ over a finite field. The proof demonstrates that every code adhering to the LCP is a direct summand of the code module, thereby generalizing prior findings found in references such as [10]. Finally, the methodology for constructing $LCP$ modules using group code methods based on abelian $p$-groups is detailed.

This paper examines electricity consumption patterns during critical periods when supply falls short of demand. Using data from Portugal in 2022, a period characterized by potential shortages, we apply a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) to analyze how factors like time of day, the inter-crisis status, socio-economic and climatic conditions influence consumption. By analyzing the interaction between power crisis periods and other variables, we identify how consumption patterns are affected. Given the non-linear dependencies between consumption and factors such as temperature and the inter-crisis status, we find temperature to be the most significant determinant of consumption variations and further develop a synthetic consumer profile to illustrate these effects. Finally, we compare the model's predictive accuracy when excluding crisis periods against simulations that account for them.

Natural language program synthesis aims to create correct code from textual specifications, including diagrams that depict algorithms through control and data flow. While existing methods primarily focus on processing linear input, diagrams offer a spatial layout containing structural information crucial for understanding the underlying logic. This research introduces a GRCNN (Graph Residual Convolutional Network) model that treats input diagrams as graphs to be identified, allowing the system to leverage graph-level features for code generation. Our method learns to synthesizing code by taking directed graphs, specific node and edge labels, and associated attributes as input. Experiments on the substantial MoDELO dataset, which contains Python programs and their corresponding flow charts, show that this graph-based approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art CNN and RNN baselines. Furthermore, gRCNN successfully generates correct programs while reducing literal count by roughly 20% and achieving a Levenshtein distance improvement of roughly 20% compared to previous state-of-the-art methods.

Our study maintains a clear perspective: the effectiveness of the tested techniques in improving forecast accuracy is evaluated based on the forecast error. We examine how error analysis informs both the assessment of model deficiencies and the development of remediation strategies designed to reduce this error. Specifically, we explore four principal approaches for addressing systematic forecast errors: correcting errors through data assimilation methods such as Ensemble Kalman Filtering; developing refined physical representations within boundary conditions and subgrid-scale processes; applying machine learning algorithms to enhance forecast capabilities; and engineering ensemble configurations aimed at minimizing bias. We offer a concise review of these methods, highlighting their mechanisms for error diminution along with associated challenges. The paper concludes by outlining promising avenues for future investigation in the field of climate model improvement.

These theoretical studies utilize a suite of software tools to analyze opacity characteristics of osmium and Au-III electron configurations, focusing on their significance in interpreting light curves from neutron star mergers. For the first time, these theories construct an Os-III spectral term diagram using a large-scale configuration interaction method with the osmium relativistic all-electron code. This diagram establishes Au-IV as an ideal one-to-one proxy, or "analog," to osmium in its third ionization state. Subsequently, employing a speed-up version of the hydrogenic all-electron RELIC code, these-:;; these-:;: we:;: construct comprehensive Opacity data sets for both elements across a broad spectrum of densities and temperatures. These datasets utilize a modern equation of state approach to calculate Planck and Rosseland mean opacities across a wide range of wavelengths and thermodynamic conditions. Finally, the study evaluates how well the Au-IV approximation serves as a proxy for osmium by comparing the spectral analyses.

This study aims to develop an automatic segmentation tool for the GI canal utilizing a deep learning framework. Rooted in Unet architecture, which excels in spatial feature extraction, the proposed model incorporates additional layers to learn hierarchical representations. Detailed in the paper are experimental outcomes, revealing a high performance with an F1 score of 0.9344.

Recent research has established a robust framework for analyzing linear mathematical properties related to compositionality in information, including vectors and matrices, with a focus on various decompositions such as the singular value decomposition (SVD), eigenvalue decomposition (EigDec), spectral value decomposition (SpecDec), and tensor decomposition (TenDec). This body of work investigates the associated eigenvalues (EnDec), stressors (SpDec), and nuclear norm decomposition (NuDec). To illustrate the significance of this mathematical foundation, the application of these concepts to the analysis of compositional information regarding the Greek alphabet is presented. Specifically, the interpretation arising from the SpecDec, which addresses compositional bias through bias correction, is highlighted as particularly meaningful.

We report on a comprehensive search for a hypothesized "habitable zone desert"—actually termed a sub-Saturn mass desert at significantly shorter periods—for super-Earths located within or near the habitable zone (HZ). Although the required sample sizes were small, these worlds were predicted based on stellar irradiation levels but expected to be scarce given the strong correlation between planetary mass and orbital period. We analyzed a radial velocity dataset comprising 211 stars with confirmed sub-Earth to Jupiter-mass companions gathered by CORALIE/HARPS. Our findings indicate no evidence of such mass desert; the distribution of stellar flux received by planets near the HZ shows no significant trend with orbital period. Consequently, sub-Saturn mass planets near their host star's HZ are likely far more numerous than the transtemporal studies of radial velocity data suggest, offering potential new insights into planet formation theories.

Regimen-based therapies are widely utilized globally for managing mental disorders, including depression. Effective deployment of these treatments relies on patients adhering to prescribed schedules, which is often compromised by disordered information processing that impedes the consistent monitoring of behavioral actions. This study introduces a novel information-theoretic framework designed to enhance treatment efficacy through improved action monitoring. We propose a method to identify actionable cues from complex, high-dimensional sensory data by maximizing mutual information between them. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting learned cue representations preserve discriminative capabilities, thereby enabling difficult attention regulation tasks. Empirical evaluations using public datasets from the University of California Irvine (UCI) confirm these advantages through analysis of real-world video footage, including those recorded in depression clinical settings.

We present a dark matter model featuring a simple spin-0 scalar that interacts with Standard Model (SM) nucleons via a Yukawa coupling to an intermediate scalar mediator. This mediator couples to pairs of oppositely charged electric particles, resulting in a sign-dependent nuclear scattering cross-section. We demonstrate that dark matter accumulation forms stable bound states when neutral, producing very narrow resonances off-shell within nucleons. Since these states decay back into dark matter and the mediator, their existence induces significant enhancements in direct detection signals. Consequently, our framework offers substantial predictions for direct detection experiments, allowing experiments to constrain dark matter annihilation rates into mediators with greater sensitivity and enabling them to probe non-conventional regions of the scattering parameter space. We utilize non-relativistic effective field theory to create efficient simulators that estimate dark matter self-interaction sections by analyzing direct detection outcomes. Furthermore, we construct explicit collider search observables within this model, allowing us to map out the parameter space using current LHC capabilities.

We investigate the possibility of achieving success across diverse biological cognitive tasks using fixed and sparse recurrent neural networks, drawing inspiration from neurobiological realities. Our findings confirm that these constraints serve as a "cognitive lottery," significantly reducing the search landscape and turning into a high probability of success. Under conditions of extreme bias favoring success, we observed an accelerated learning rate across various architectures and functions, thereby reducing training time. This approach achieved success on tasks simulating real biological processes—including olfactory discrimination, sequence modeling based on DNA and disaccharides patterns, predicting interDNA forces, and generating synthetic brain activity—alongside standard benchmarks like language prediction and image classification. When trained end-to-end, these models demonstrated the ability to extract meaningful temporal structures from synthetic data and learned to anticipate future positions in sequences derived from the human vocabulary.

Radio- and X-ray-emitting Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) represent a significant population throughout cosmic history, with many instances detected at extreme redshifts ($z >$ 6). The mechanisms driving their early ignition and subsequent growth remain uncertain. This study utilizes the cosmological simulation "21cmCosmo" to model the cumulative influence of C-band (2.1 cm) and X-ray (0.1 keV) radiation on the thermal and chemical evolution of primordial gas. We examined how AGN feedback alters star formation rates and chemical enrichment, comparing our findings to an control model devoid of these influences. Our results indicate that the inverse Compton cooling modification operates on a timescale of 1–2 Gyr, gradually triggering and regulating the emergence of the observed radio- and X-ray-luminous AGN populations at high redshifts. Concurrently, the intrinsically quenching power of the relativistic jets associated with these early AGN helps to regulate star formation and chemical enrichment in the subsequent $z \approx 5–7$ epoch.

We explore several aspects of scalar field Lagrangians capable of facilitating a classical description of gravitation. Linearity in scalar field derivatives is a common characteristic of these models. We examine the possibilities for promoting the amplitude, which in the simplest case represents the Newtonian gravitational constant $G_{\rm N}$, from a fixed parameter to a dynamical entity. We outline general principles and strategies for achieving this promotion and analyze specific applications. In particular, we demonstrate promotion within Einstein-Hilbert action via two methods: a Verheijden-type term proposed by Bekenstein and Vermeiden and through Gaussian fluctuations of quantum metrics. We further discuss an alternative effective gravity framework where effective amplitudes for coupling parameters are determined by solving algebraic equations. These solutions, representing physically viable roots, define viable coupling strengths. We assess the stability of these solutions in both slow-varying and rapidly varying regimes. Finally, we investigate scenarios where these coupling strengths vary spatially or temporally, analyzing additional effects in static space-times that possess a Killing vector.

This study introduces a new approach for aligning 3D medical image datasets, derived from extending the 2D SIFT methodology. While the extension introduces modifications, its core depends heavily on the original 2D version. A primary factor in the success of these techniques is the quality of the feature detector; in our work, this role is fulfilled by the 3D-SIFT detector. However, matching these features can introduce noise that degrades alignment accuracy. To resolve this, we implemented a post-processing step that filters out inaccurate descriptors using distance-to-plane metrics within the match database. Furthermore, leveraging descriptor descriptor rotation invariance allows us to extract spatial position and orientation data from the features themselves. We apply discrete sparse principal component analysis to this orientation information to create a symmetry-based cost metric; descriptors with inconsistent spatial relationships across volumes incur higher costs. Although a full volumetric 3D SIFT process is computationally heavy, our method proves highly effective on practical picture layers.

Global aggregation techniques, such as mean, median, and Jaccard distance, are essential for preserving privacy and enabling multi-party computation as well as machine learning over distributed data; however, they suffer from suboptimal privacy guarantees against high entropy data and inefficiently utilize information when data types are heterogeneous. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a general framework utilizing Wasserstein distances that supports various applications of global aggregation, offering provably stronger privacy and higher information retention. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by proving privacy advantages for categorical, numerical, and multi-dimensional data—whether independent or correlated—and by designing an innovative median aggregation method based on a categorical type-space graph that achieves better both privacy and accuracy than current alternatives. Additionally, the proposed system allows users to release auxiliary, non-sensitive data without compromising privacy or data utility, provided it adheres to a specified level of privacy. Finally, we expose critical flaws in an existing proposed method by Zhang et al. concerning the release of auxiliary information, and furthermore, we prove that aggregation and auxiliary release are mutually exclusive objectives within their specific proposed architecture.

**Purpose:** We aimed to examine the morphological characteristics and AGN accretion rates by analyzing the relationship between AGN types and host galaxies using the GALEX, SDSS, and IRXDS surveys data.

**Methods:** We utilized the GALEX and SDSS surveys data to determine the sample's inclination and optical morphology. Furthermore, we employed the IRXDS database to validate our findings.

**Results:** Our analysis indicates that the optical morphology and host inclination of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) vary according to their classification. Specifically, Radio-Quiet Quasars exhibit the steepest host inclinations, whereas Radio-Quiet Seyferts display the least host inclinations.

**Conclusions:** The optical morphology and host inclination of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are not distributed randomly; their differences across various AGN types provide additional constraints on the "Dust Obscured" model.

This paper introduces TCube, a framework dedicated to time-series storytelling. Given a set of metrics, TCube takes multiple input time-series signals, identifies key events occurring within the data, and utilizes event kernels to render the narrative visually. The resulting composition offers both a natural language description and a dynamic visualization that aids user comprehension. To achieve this, the system employs two key components: an event detection module trained on a synthetic dataset to identify patterns without reliance on domain-specific knowledge, and a natural language generation (LLM) pipeline that maps these patterns and the time-series context into summary text, using synthetic data to generate diverse samples. The creation of this synthetic dataset involved the use of a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize realistic time series. Testing across various domains—including finance, industry, and physiology—demonstrated that the domain-neutral nature of the model allows it to perform effectively without fine-tuning, and the quality of the generated stories was validated by subject experts.

The ATLAS collaboration presents updated limits on CP violation in bottom charm mesons, as well as new constraints regarding the branching fractions of rare beauty hadron decays. For the analysis of bottom charm mesons, the study utilizes tagged $B_{s}^{0}\to D^{\pm} D^{\mp}\bar{c}X$ events to locate peaks within the invariant mass distribution. This allows for the extraction of the oscillation frequency $\mathcal{M}_{d}^{*}$ using the angular profile of the decay orientation relative to the oscillation axis. An oscillation is observed with a significance reaching 13 sigma, yielding a measured or inferred mean oscillation period $\mathcal{M}_{d}^{*}$ of approximately 0.33 ps$^{-1}$ from 2015 LHC data collected at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 36 fb$^{-1}$. When assuming a constant decay probability per oscillation, no statistical evidence for CP violation was found. We examine the Ising model defined on a Cayley tree and under an external magnetic field exhibiting a mild variation. By applying a mild variation to the tree's labeling, we analyze how this factor influences the tree's boundaries at level $n$, specifically demonstrating that these boundaries transition from simply connected to genus-one surfaces. Under these conditions, we discover new mild-variation-periodic Gibbs measures that were absent when considering non-periodic cases. Finally, we derive sufficient criteria determining when these newly found measures are unique among their class.

Recent research by Card et al. introduces a valuable methodological framework—the Inverted Luttig-Robinson (LIR) method—for instrumental variables (IV) analysis in scenarios where multiple endogenous treatments coexist, a technique later popularized by Bona et al. This study providesnovel theoretical insights into how to properly identify causal effects using LIR when treatment variables are discrete, employing a nonparametric, preference-based model grounded in the latent variable model of Haile and Muellbauer. We demonstrate that when considering IVs uncorrelated with observed or unobserved confounders, the proposed framework yields up to \(T+1\) distinct point-identifications, whereas instruments correlated with unobserved correlations result in set identification. These findings extend and refine earlier work by Bona and colleagues. Applying this approach to data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Freshmen (NLSF), we analyze how college major selection influences wage outcomes. Using this unique preference-driven model, we derive testable implications for this problem, including the observation that valid reduced-form estimates from unrelated instrumental variables must align with those derived using preference-informed instrumental variables. Finally, we provide evidence supporting more positive, yet still modest, causal effects of choosing unrelated fields on the part of individuals who enter the university with an intention to pursue physics.

The ongoing charm factory projects provide access to a collection of exotic hadrons, notably by facilitating the production of the J/ψ resonance. Although numerous collisions yield J/ψ plants of various types, they unfortunately remain largely unstable and decay rapidly, precluding their use as primary sources for particles. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative strategy involving the employment of magnetic lenses to efficiently isolate and concentrate these unconventional hadrons into a singular, high-flux output. By applying this lens system to the filtering process, we can achieve the generation of a particle plant characterized specifically by the presence of abundant antineutrons, both anti-hyperons and hypertons, alongside high levels of purity. Such a novel high-energy physics facility, designed specifically to study these special particles with unprecedented precision, holds significant promise for revealing novel decay modes, discovering new resonances, and providing important insights into the complex mechanisms governing dark matter behavior. Our research suggests that achieving this highly precise and pure species of anti-particles requires the utilization of modern lens technologies with superior performance characteristics.

We have developed a numerical model to simulate the accretion dynamics of growing black hole binaries within hierarchical triple systems that possess circumstellar disks. In our framework, in-fall rates are calculated using analytic profiles, which subsequently determine the evolution of the inner disk and the recycling of mass from the disk onto the inner binary components. Our results indicate that when the system is initially configured with a tight outer triple, disks are efficiently depleted on a timescale of approximately 100 million years, causing the outer binary to evolve significantly inward. Conversely, when wide triples are used as starting conditions, inner binary evolution dominates over disk-driven processes, with mass depletion in that configuration taking roughly 1 billion years. Throughout these simulations, we observe a pronounced rise in both Eddington fractions and Eddington-limited phases for the symbiotic X-ray sources immediately following the event where the inner binary swallows its companion star, whereas standard X-ray binaries never reach such high luminosity limits.

Image restoration is crucial in numerous applications, yet traditional methods often fail to recover high-quality results in the presence of severe degradation. This paper introduces a new variance image model that integrates state-of-the-art restoration techniques with modern deep-learning approaches. Specifically, we utilize a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to serve as a variance estimator for nonhomogeneous areas, thereby enabling more accurate segmentation. Following this variance modeling, we apply a Poisson-based mixing technique to partition images into multiple distinct parts. Subsequently, each individual part is reconstructed independently using the Minimum Entog-Cvar (ENC) method, which is recognized for its simplicity and high efficiency, thereby yielding superior restoration outcomes on heterogeneous images compared to prior studies. To validate the proposed framework, this study implements the model on synthetic and real-world datasets, with results confirmed through quantitative analysis supporting the method's high effectiveness.

We leverage astrophysical observations to place new constraints on ultralight self-gravitating bosonic dark matter. By applying a simple model that accounts for the quasar spin-growth via accretion—specifically linking final spin values to their respective lifetimes and accretion histories within a $\Lambda$CDM framework—we re-evaluate the parameter space for the mass of an ultralight boson by analyzing how much the accretion history broadens the excluded region compared to previous limits derived under the assumption of instantaneous spin-down. When applied to periods between quasars' spin down events, these broadened limits offer approximately $20\%$ additional exclusion coverage. By considering multiple accretion episodes across the quasar spin evolution, we derive timing-dependent bounds on the boson's mass. For a universe age of $12$~Gyr, this approach yields constraints on the dark photon's mass within the range of $10^{-17}$~eV$< m_\phi < 10^{-14}$~eV.

Creating artificial neuromorphic systems involves defining a set of spiking neurons and plasticity rules to solve computational issues, constrained by execution on hardware that may diverge from ideal theoretical designs due to intrinsic physical limitations. Atom-based sensors driven by trapped spin states exhibit remarkable sensitivity for detecting fields, which far exceeds current capabilities of standard technology. Although these sensors offer exceptional precision, the challenge of trapping atoms remains an external bottleneck that hinders their real-world deployment. We introduce and experimentally validate a fully integrated planar micro-magnetic trap capable of capturing magnetically negative atoms, effectively removing this hardware barrier. Our experimentally demonstrated trap features an area as small as $1.3 \, \mu\mathrm{m}$ wide with an attraction force reaching the magnitude of $-30 \, \mathrm{pN}$. These results establish a new framework for enabling self-assembled, highly sensitive atom-based sensing technologies on-chip.

This study examines the accretion of a stationary fluid onto a Schwarzschild black hole, starting with an inflow that possesses finite dimensions. We model the fluid using both a perfect pressure approach and a kinetic framework, addressing the latter via a one-dimensional Fokker-Planck equation while accounting for its associated rotational momentum. Our findings indicate that a stationary fluid dynamics solution exists for all momentum distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a local enthalpy flux maximum serves as the threshold separating open from closed trajectories. Analyzing the role of rotational momentum, our results reveal an m-fold periodic dependence regarding the existence of closed orbits, where m represents the number of velocity levels with non-zero distribution. We utilize both analytical methods and numerical analysis to determine the boundaries of the domain defining the system's momentum, position, and radial velocities required to generate these orbits across different black hole masses. Additionally, we evaluate how the black hole's event horizon influences the critical enthalpy flux value by examining how it modifies both accretion rates and outflow mass loss.

We investigate the spontaneous emission of a point dipole facing a slender metallic mirror to explore how geometry influences light-matter interaction. Our findings reveal that a point dipole positioned against a narrow mirror exhibits different dynamics compared to one facing a planar mirror; specifically, the decay rate is modified based on the relative orientation between the dipole and the mirror. At a distance of roughly one hundred nanometers from a mirror with a width of 500 nm, the decay rate can vary by up to 100%. Additionally, the emitted spectrum shows a geometric dependence that shifts significantly when the dipole moves, changing on a scale of approximately 100 nP. Furthermore, when a moving dipole faces the slender mirror, it generates a classical electromagnetic signal whose intensity scales with both velocity and the square of the dipole moment. This emission arises from geometric charge polarization caused within the mirror material by the dipole's motion.

It considers the case with a exponential type critical growth condition and identifies localized solutions by minimizing a constrained energy functional. Handwritten document images (HDIs) are frequently compromised by distortions such as skewed perspectives, uneven lighting, noisy textures, and handwritten occlusions. These artifacts significantly hinder performance for downstream tasks like handwritten recognition, despite the availability of advanced deep learning models that have largely overcome challenges related to natural variation in HI acquisition while struggling with degraded input quality. To address this limitation, we introduce a multi-task adversarial network designed to enhance HI quality across three distinct stages: skew correction, line separation, and ink removal. Specifically, line separation and skew correction modules collectively align text lines and orient them horizontally, allowing the subsequent refiner to focus exclusively on removing ink while assuming textual structure is already regular. Our system demonstrates superior efficiency in clearing ink marks compared to existing methods, notably those lacking integration with preprocessing steps. Furthermore, the trained models yield substantial performance gains in HPR tasks, successfully denoting documents and recovering separated character information.

Identifying individuals is crucial for various reasons, including identifying victims of human trafficking, facilitating voter registration, and assisting law enforcement in solving crimes. In Indonesia, the primary method for identification is through ID cards, which hold legal standing. These documents contain essential details such as the holder's name, birth date, and birthplace, all of which are electronically stored as image files issued by the government. While ID card issuance volumes have surged across the nation, digitizing these massive datasets has not kept pace, resulting in numerous critical information gaps. Consequently, this research introduces a novel hybrid system designed to automate the extraction of metadata from Indonesian ID card images. By integrating government specifications, this study introduces a new stage for validation, ensuring the accuracy of extracted data. The implemented technology achieves an average precision and recall of 90.5% and 88.9%, respectively, while running at 0.95 F1-score.

In Light Vehicle to Infrastructure (V2I) communication, a critical component of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), ensuring high fidelity channel estimation is essential for maintaining reliable IEEE 802.11p links, which are inherently susceptible to rapid fluctuations. To enhance the traditional Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) method, this study introduces an improved scheme leveraging Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks for enhanced temporal smoothing alongside standard MMSE data. By utilizing past channels and error estimates, the LSTM-based phase refines the standard MMSE output. Simulation results demonstrate the superior performance of this combined approach, particularly in scenarios with low sub-carrier counts where the traditional method may falter under high estimation error rates compared to these improved capabilities.

Picture colorization serves as a well-known, highly influential, and extensively researched image editing task within computer vision. In contrast to this established research focus, its application to scientific (e.g., satellite) imagery remains a nascent field. This paper details an investigation into utilizing image colorization, in particular, to amplify visual fidelity in both visibility-limited and time-resolved satellite data. The study evaluates a variety of colorization techniques and documents the integration of an ImageGAN to further elevate the results. Additionally, a novel, specialized Colorization Assisted Interpretation (CAIE) framework is introduced, which combines deep-learning based colorization with image super-resolution and a new method for highlighting important features in monochromatic data sets. Extensive testing confirms that CAIE substantially improves observation clarity, effectively reducing noise, and significantly boosts readability.

This study introduces a new finitely wide feedforward neural network architecture designed for regression tasks. This structure utilizes separately parameterized activation functions and activation biases, governed by $k$ shared sets of weights, each of which have an $n$-dimensional vector form. The work proves that this neural network is universally approximating: for any square-integrable target function on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and an infinite set of samples $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ drawn from $\Omega$, there exists a separate, convergent path for the network's parameters that causes its prediction error to vanish as sample count $n$ increases. Furthermore, under the assumption of i.i.d. sampling from a distribution on $\Omega$, the error probability converges to zero according to the law of large numbers, and subsequently to a Gaussian distribution as error approaches zero. The analysis extends to scenarios where the input data $\{x_i\}$ follows a band-limited prior, yielding specific rates of error convergence dependent on $n$ and $k$. These theoretical findings rest on the application of Stochastic Taylor expansions and are supported by numerical experiments. The proposed architecture employs optimization-free training methods, thereby streamlining computation.

In 2021, the ECFA established its Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCR) to engage and advocate for the interests of early career scholars. Comprising 35 members, many of whom are now active researchers, this committee has organized multiple events and initiatives over the last two years. This paper provides the first comprehensive overview detailing our formation and the specific activities undertaken between January 2021 and December 2022.

Line defects within the framework of electromagnetic metamaterials have been shown to facilitate line wave propagation. The demonstrated capability to controll the dispersion and complex nature of this metam Line wave through strategic design highlights its vast potential for optical metasurfaces and integrated devices. To achieve this, we present a capable and adaptable metastructure that guides line waves along path of interest while exhibiting a negative, dispersion-independent dispersion. Consequently, this metamaterial line wave demonstrates its capability for extraordinary transmission, thereby broadening the scope of optical metamaterials and related technologies.

We introduce COGLAB, an open-source cognitive architecture designed to simulate human-robot collaborative scenarios. Developed to accelerate scientific progress, this platform features visual programming capabilities that enable the rapid construction of accessibly coded agent models with significant complexity. By facilitating the simulation of many-large-scale interactions between humans and robots or in multi-agent/robot teams, COGLAB supports the introduction of new behavioral theories. The architecture integrates established cognitive theories, including working memory, a declarative memory grounded in Bayesian principles, and mechanisms like attention and metacognition. This paper outlines our experiences utilizing this environment in the joint mastery of a bimanual manipulation task between a human and robot. Additionally, to validate its extensibility, a novel mechanism for social learning through imitation from one or more peers—whether human or robotic—is implemented within the system.

The population median and mean absolute deviation are preferred nonparametric counterparts to parametric estimates of location and scale. Despite this, joint point estimation for these metrics often suffers from substantial bias, particularly in small samples, which has led to the historical neglect of confidence interval research for these parameters. This study addresses that oversight by introducing a bias-reduced inference method via the Delphi algorithm to calculate asymptotically accurate confidence intervals. The approach's efficacy is validated using simulated data and a real-world dataset, demonstrating that the proposed intervals offer comparable accuracy to asymptatically valid intervals generated by bootstrap resampling.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying semantic connections, defined as relationships between subjects and objects within the context of a sentence. Despite existing RE studies have integrated external knowledge to aid decision-making, recent approaches often fail to adequately leverage this info. We address this limitation through a dual-knowledge-use strategy: first, we enrich training and test datasets to make the model more robust; second, we incorporate external knowledge directly into the predictive algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a relational triplet encoder utilizing transformer architecture to learn logical and semantic links from knowledge graphs. This encoder feeds into a relation classification module based on tensor-truthed representation learning for joint relation extraction. By applying k-step reasoning to these learned triplets, we perform monstic knowledge inference. Our experiments on English datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline systems, effectively highlighting the benefits of incorporating knowledge graphs into both training data and the predictive process simultaneously.

The uncontrolled thermal and chemical potentials, combined with momentum-anisotropy, characterize the novel extreme environment of ultra-relativistic heavy ion and proton-proton collisions. This study examines quarkonium fragmentation within this medium, where the momentum-dependent anisotropy is implemented into the hot Debye mass and quark self-energies, alongside finite-baryon chemical potential effects on the heavy quark effective potential. The analysis investigates the impact of these factors on quarkonium survival probabilities across various temperatures, chemical potentials, and spatial dimensions. The results indicate that heavy quarkonium dissociation is suppressed by increasing chemical potential and spatial dimensions, while the momentum-anisotropy exhibits a non-monotonic influence on quarkonium dissociation. Additionally, spatial dimensions in an odd vs. even configuration produce distinct behaviors; specifically, lower temperatures correlate with higher survival probabilities in even-dimensional spaces, whereas the opposite trend is observed in odd dimensions.

Representing input data is a foundational challenge in machine learning, where a desirable outcome is a low-dimensional set of features that capture the intrinsic structure of the data manifold. Achieving intrinsic low dimensionality often implies generalization capabilities, enabling functions learned on these representations to extend to unseen data contexts effectively. However, conventional neural network training prioritizes performance over general theory, often neglecting guarantees against unknown data contexts. This paper proposes a recurrent architecture designed to generalize by orchestrating two distinct representational layers: the first encodes data into a space with intrinsic low dimensionality, while the second maps these representations to task outputs. Within this framework, static context-independent data locations are modeled as recurrent weights modulating signals derived from time-varying contexts at varying speeds. This modulating mechanism constitutes a novel recurrent function approximation strategy, establishing new bounds on the ability to learn composite functions by separating them into a static recurrence component and a dynamic modulation part. Specifically, functions are constructed by combining static mappings from high-dimensional inputs to low-dimensional states with linear operators parameterized by those states. We demonstrate that the joint composition of these elements can approximate continuous functions over static inputs and their permutation with continuous paths across dynamic contexts, provided the underlying static data distribution is confined to a low-effective-dimensional region.

Current methods for synthetic data generation and downstream tasks are typically designed for static datasets and often fail to handle dynamic real-world environments where data distributions shift over time. This paper introduces a new class of statistical models, termed semi-generative covering the causal layers of features and outcomes, designed to address generation and task performance under covariate shift. This framework outperforms state-of-the-art approaches for both generative tasks and prediction. This paper introduces the semi-generative model, designed with an implicit structure to separate feature dependencies across causal pathways while maintaining explicit expressions for features, unobserved confounders, effects, and result variables. We show that this model can address the problem of independent identically distributed sample generation while simultaneously providing optimal prediction for target variables, considering the presence of covariate shift. We also provide the theoretical results supporting the performance of this model. Finally, we offer two novel algorithms for deep neural network-based neural network implementation of this probabilistic model, achieving superior performance over existing methods for both generation and tasks.

We investigate the successful deployment of deep learning in diverse fields, primarily by examining the underlying geometric principles that enable these methods to work. This study focuses on two central aspects: the proximity of nearest neighbors and the connectivity of level sets, both of which are critical to why deep learning is so effective, often being conflated with manifold learning yet under-explored in standard textbooks. To illustrate these concepts, we employ prisms, pyramids, and cones as primitive geometric models. Although these shapes are not manifold, they approximate various manifolds in specific contexts, and more importantly, they share similar topological and differential geometric characteristics that help explain the mechanisms of the methods we analyze. We argue that a thorough understanding of these properties is as essential as mastering the historical algorithms and theoretical proofs of the field.

We define a set of grid functions influenced by a parameter $t$, grounded in our new definition of main factor. By employing the well-established well-spaced point system within these grids, we avoid the convergence issues typically associated with classical point definitions to enhance calculation precision and efficiency. This framework allows us to examine properties related to three critical elements: main factor, higher-order minimum, and well-ordering principle. Additionally, we utilize the established minimum term of higher-order to describe grid functions more comprehensively. Through this theoretical foundation, we derive several new results regarding hyperquarter and hyperquarter functions.

This paper applies Layerwise Relevance Propagation (LRP) within a layered deep learning framework (LRP-DNN) to analyze a Deep Neural Network (DNN) employed in a recent study for classifying high-energy particle jets. The methodology involves tracing every output relevance unit backward through the network to determine the specific input jet constituents responsible for a given classification decision. By utilizing an expert-variable framework, we successfully reconstructed a qualitative class-representative "class prototype," effectively demonstrating the neural concept underlying the network's classification logic. This approach revealed a strong affinity between the generated prototype structure and the intuitive physical model currently employed by experts in jet physics. Furthermore, LRP-DNN successfully decomposed relevance into two distinct physical components representing both non-linear features and features with linear characteristics.

In this study, we introduce and analyze two novel sequence families named the degenerate $r$-linked Stirling numbers of the second kind and the degenerate linked Stirling numbers of the first kind. We establish recurrence relations, various identities, and zero-term properties for these numbers. Furthermore, we derive methods to represent polynomial expansions using degenerate linked Stirling numbers and examine connections between our proposed numbers and Bell polynomials.

Perceptual shifts triggered by virtual reality have attracted growing interest from neuroscientists, though their potential use as modalities for examining altered states of consciousness remains under-explored. These perceptual turns may stem from shifts in neural processing resulting from VR-induced sensory manipulation, or they could serve as manifestations of emerging altered states of awareness. In order to investigate this mechanism, a study enrolling 18 participants examined visual detection thresholds within an immersive VR environment under both standard conditions and those simulating shadow ingestion. Findings revealed that while participants exhibited no change in discriminative acuity for Gabor patches whenVR-enabled compared to non-VR setups during baseline, they demonstrated a perceptually significant elevation in thresholds when exposed to shadow aspects. This same sensitivity increase was also documented under non-immersive visual monitoring. The results suggest VR-shadow ingestion triggers distinct perceptual alterations comparable to those seen elsewhere in literature, possibly linked to GABA-mediated modulation of excitatory-inhibitory balance in cortical circuits, thereby reinforcing the utility of VR systems in researching altered states of mind.

We introduce an adaptation of BigScience's multilingual model to support inference in unwritten languages. We modify the code to add a new language identifier, extend the training data loader to accommodate additional data formats, and implement a data augmentation strategy. Our findings indicate that this cost-effective approach effectively enables the use of resources in languages for which the original pre-trained framework had no support.

Direct Collapse Binaries (DCBs) arising from the direct collapse of massive stars are considered the most viable source for gravitational waves detected by LIGO and future detectors. A key unresolved issue concerns the creation of these binary systems. This study utilizes direct numerical simulations to examine the formation of DCBs, specifically focusing on the fragmentation of a single, rapidly spinning, high-mass core. As the core accumulates additional accreted mass and becomes increasingly unstable, it undergoes a violent break-up, splitting into a pair of secondary bodies. These secondaries form a binary orbiting the system's center of mass. A key characteristic is that the sum of the secondary masses roughly equals the original mass, implying that mass is not conserved in a simple additive sense or is lost through fragmentation. A valuable byproduct of our analysis is a set of scaling relations for the mass of the secondary bodies as functions of the primary mass and spin parameter. These relationships enable predictions of binary mass configurations, although they assume a 2-body fragmentation outcome. Furthermore, our findings suggest a potential link between the final binary mass distribution and the initial conditions, specifically the mass and radius of the nascent protostar.

This investigation explores a newly introduced class of distributions, known as m-araknlovian (m-A-R), which generalizes the well-studied araknlovian property within univariate distributions to the multivariate domain. These distributions arise as linear combinations of independent components, each following an independent and identically distributed law and integrated over the general linear group. Analysis reveals that this family encompasses diverse distribution types, including those that are not strictly sub-gaussian. Given the functional similarity to existing self-decomposable multivariate concepts, the new class shares notable characteristics with them. We provide an extensive framework for identifying suitable parameters and density functions for m-ar-k distributions. Critically, this research investigates the applicability of M-ar-k models to the problem of independent component analysis in a way that guarantees rapid convergence. Specifically, it has been determined that M-ar-k models facilitate fast convergence for the algorithm proposed by Masonnet al., thereby enabling efficient statistical inference even in the context of heavy-tailed distributions.

From this analysis, we derive new CPT characterizations based on limited Herbrand models. In choosing these illustrative cases, we examined the intersection of choiceless polynomial time with first-order logic over bounded primitives—a area we believe has been underexplored. These structural insights offer significant implications for understanding the boundaries between CPT, CPR, first-order logic, and choiceless logic, particularly within the framework of bounded graphs where we also compare these theories against extended polynomial calculus (EPC). This study examines the relative similarity and structural intricacy of positions within the chess opening repertoire, leveraging a dataset of games gathered from an online chess community. By utilizing the SGFN (Shortest-Go Form Tree) representation for chess games, the researchers employed spectral tree embedding to create high-dimensional position features. These embeddings were then fed into both supervised and unsupervised clustering techniques to organize similar positions. Finally, the proposed methods were validated through an experiment where human experts identified the plausibility of moves, thereby assessing the methods' validity.

This study introduces the derivation of key millisecond pulsar parameters by extending existing methods to pulsar-powered supernovae, utilizing the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) applied to white dwarf remnants. Our findings indicate that when applied in conjunction with standard models, AIC effectively determines ejection velocities, ejecta masses, and the total energy input from the pulsar. Furthermore, when the model incorporates an isotope composition dependent on a pulsar-powered phase, these capabilities expand to include constraints on the radius of the central remant, pulsar spin periods, and the timescale for that emission.

This study examines the applicability of various degree-based nonlocal theories within the framework of Lagrangian systems. The analysis reveals two key insights: (1) every nonlocal law of motion, regardless of its degree, admits an equivalent variational principle involving a nonlocal action integral; (2) there exists a general nonlocal Hamiltonian formulation applicable across all degrees of nonlocality. This principle holds true in both continuous field theories and discrete models, including those describing matter fields, scalar fields, electromagnetic fields, as well as systems with finite degrees of freedom.

Virtual Reality (VR) technology has proven highly effective for spatial visualization across numerous fields, particularly excelling in areas like medical imaging and industrial maintenance. Despite these successes, core 3D VR interaction methods remain limited, often relying primarily on free-flying models or surface drawing techniques. This study introduces a new interaction paradigm: surfacing 3D object creation from virtual sketched trails. Utilizing a head-mounted display (HMD) and a single handheld tracker, the method translates drawings made on the air screen into 3D geometric primitives, where each sketch functions as the surface of the final object. The process infers shapes through user input of specific dimensions, such as width and height. Upon completion, an algorithm matches the created 3D object against a centralized library for immediate retrieval. We validated this approach using a custom-constructed scene set, assessing both the generation precision and the performance of the subsequent data retrieval system.

The study of gravitational collapse in ideal fluids with linear equations of state, particularly those derived using the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations, has been a major area of focus. However, recent research has uncovered an inconsistency: applying a linear equation of state within this traditional "isentropic" collapse model leads to a non-feasible TOV equation system. This contradiction arises because such an equation of state causes the density to approach infinity at all radii, rendering a static configuration impossible. Consequently, an isentropic collapse based on linear equations of state cannot consistently yield a black hole or neutron star solution.

We utilize the Iyer-Wald formalism to revisit and broaden analyses of extremal black holes within a four-dimensional static, spherically symmetric framework. Although our findings align with previous studies for the standard cases of Einstein gravity coupled with electromagnetic fields, the method proves more versatile when addressing more complex scenarios, specifically higher-derivative gravity theories and scenarios lacking a finite mass in the non-extremal limit.

Current deep reinforcement learning methods for controlling actuated devices often apply learning directly to the robot's joint angles. Yet, this approach suffers from high dimensionality and significant nonlinearity, creating notable obstacles for effective motor acquisition. Alternatively, learning within the device's end-effector space offers advantages by operating in a lower-dimensional environment that remains more fetcher, thereby enhancing performance. Although this strategy diminishes the risk of damaging internal components by shielding the joints from excessive stress or damage, existing approaches tend to cause such internal risks. Consequently, we introduce the Final Effector Investigation Drive, specifically designed to promote successful motor acquisition while preventing potential internal harm to the device's inner structure. The core of our proposal relies on a Jacobian-guided representation that enables a linear transformation from joints to the end-effector space. Furthermore, a learned device model forecasts joint velocities based on the difference between current target goals and achieved outcomes; this component is integrated into the reward function to diminish stress on the inner mechanism. Experimental validation on a real-world manipulator demonstrates both effective task execution and a significant reduction in joint activity. Additionally, our framework supports diverse goal configurations, thereby enhancing robustness against environmental changes.
