An upward planar drawing of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is one where every directed edge extends from a lower to a higher position. For a long time, it remained unknown whether the problem of determining upward planarity could be solved in linear time. We present a new approach based on partial permutations that is parameterized by the graph width. We demonstrate that, given a fixed graph width, we can decide planar upward drawings of the resulting DAGs in linear time. Furthermore, we show how to generate a valid drawing—or confirm non-existence—in $O(m \log n)$ time. Our methodology finds broad application within the family of upward planarity problems. We validate this finding by examining two specific types: weakly and strongly planar DAGs, as well as transitively orientable graphs. In each case, our framework yields time-efficient algorithms for decision tasks linear with respect to the total number of edges.

Previous works in visual navigation have often treated memory as unlimited or have selected memory cache entries only based on how closely they match the current view. These approaches fail to take advantage of the inherent compactness found within natural image segments. This paper introduces MemoNav, an agent capable of navigating an ego-navigation setting while selectively recalling informative image patches to support decision-making. By applying an epistemically motivated choice criterion, the agent decides what to remember according to how much an experience would reduce uncertainty regarding its belief in the correct navigation strategy. This process enables the agent to actively choose knowledge acquisitions most valuable for learning. Additionally, an unsupervised pre-training method is proposed to create synthetic datasets of memory banks by extracting meaningful image patches. Finally, an end-to-end trainable system is developed using a large, synthesized memory bank, demonstrating that a curated large-scale memory bank can benefit agent performance and that an active policy of memory selection surpasses passive benchmarks. Code and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/razielzhang/memonav.

The demand for high-quality, high-speed data connectivity has driven the transition from 4G to 5G, with future 6G networks poised to further elevate this standard. The mobile offloading capabilities of these evolving generations have sparked significant interest in deploying Heterogeneous Networks (HETNs) within mobile backhaul (MB) frameworks. This paper reviews the evolution of this trend, tracing the shift of small cells from their inception in 4G through the 5G deployment to prospective applications in 6G. It comprehensively analyzes small-cell advantages, challenges, and 4G/5G standardization before detailing the advanced features and potential benefits of large-scale small-cell deployments in 6G. Ultimately, this work evaluates the performance of next-generation tiny-cell architectures in 6G, highlighting the trajectory of these technologies across different generational standards.

Hypergraphs offer a versatile framework for modeling multi-way relationships, extending graph theory in much the same way that graphs generalize relations. This expository chapter will survey current research on dynamic and wireless hypergraph structures, emphasizing concepts related to stability and coloring within these dynamic environments.

This study explores how quantum field theory operators entangle through their mode expansions, specifically within free theories where mode selection is conventional. By applying tomographic techniques, we quantify entanglement for tomograms of Tomographic Hamiltonian models (the Hamiltonian itself, not a model). The analysis reveals that in standard theories (such as those with standard mode definitions), entanglement remains invariant under unitary transformations involving tomographic measurements. Using tomogram-based entanglement measures, we apply these concepts to scalar fields, but the methodology is general and applies to any system described by tomograms.

The structural theory regarding how massive stars form low-metallicity environments relies on estimating parameters for a specific nuclear reaction: the direct decay of the Hoyle state in $^8$He to three alpha particles ($\alpha^3$). This study introduces the first experimental measurement of this process within a Time Projection Chamber (TPC) environment. By utilizing the inherent self-triggering capabilities of the chamber alongside its superior measurement precision, the research achieved the process isolation from background interference, achieving near-zero background levels. Based on these results, the scientific team derived the primary value for the Hoyle direct-decay coefficient, establishing a dataset that empowers the calculation of the associated astrophysical factor $S_{Hoyle}$ with an uncertainty margin of up to one order of magnitude less than previous estimates. This precise determination of the $S_{Hoyle}$ constant provides necessary accuracy for astrophysical models predicting carbon synthesis in stellar environments.

Addressing the limitations of atomistic simulations, which struggle to fracture due to artificial 2D material boundaries, we developed a new method to fracture boundary-free 2D solids. This approach models fracture as the propagation of a tip along the periphery of a virtual island generated by a phase-field order parameter, utilizing both intrinsic material length and characteristic time scales that are absent in traditional bulk materials. This innovation allows for the investigation of fracture in geometrically unconstrained solids, potentially enabling the identification of new applications for this class of structures.

This study examines communication channels that depend on state and are modeled as finite-state conduits, where internal states update according to an autonomous rule driven by past and present channel inputs. These channels represent significant developments of classical memoryless Gaussian models and effectively capture broader stochastic phenomena found in practical scenarios such as turbulence-induced Gaussian channels and magnetic storage media. We analyze a specific scenario where both encoder and decoder possess full knowledge of channel states. Under these conditions, where access to shared randomness is assumed, we derive closed-form expressions for the achievable rate region and demonstrate the necessity of some form of this information at the encoder to guarantee non-zero communication rates. Our proposed achievable region leverages a "feedback-driven finite-state conduit," which is essentially a directed weighted graph optimized to transmit information. We demonstrate how to construct these graphs using spectral factorization and a maximum-weight matching algorithm. Notably, our findings reveal that a codebook utilizing randomly assigned states at the encoder offers strictly superior performance compared to a random selection of codes.

Recent theoretical work suggests that adding a Rashba spin-orbit coupling term to an attractive Hubbard model could induce a phase transition from a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) state to a spin singlet superfluid phase, potentially enabling superfluidity without a magnetic field. In this study, however, a phase diagram analysis using second-order perturbation theory—valid for weak interactions—is combined with numerical Monte Carlo simulations to investigate this transition. The results reveal a consistency between these methods: they identify a low-density, zero-temperature region in the phase diagram where the ground state is a $d_{x^2-y^2}$ spin singlet superfluid. Notably, the zero-temperature ground state fails to be this $d_{x^2-y^2}$ superfluid once the particle density surpasses a critical threshold. Instead, it transitions to the standard spin triplet s-wave BCS state. A similar zero-temperature behavior was observed for the $p_{x}$ superfluid ground state in square-lattice systems with dimerization. Additionally, at finite temperatures, this $p_{x}$ superfluid phase extends over a broader region of the phase diagram compared to the low-density singless states, suggesting its potential experimental viability.

We explain the intrinsic necessity of these numbers within linear operators to preserve both time translation and spatial parity, as well as their contribution to maintaining time reversibility. Particular attention is paid to how complex numbers facilitate the representation of the additive group of the wave. Furthermore, the paper explores the significance of complex phase shifts in scattering theories and matrix formulations, highlighting their capacity to characterize the additive group of the wave.

This generalized parameter considers B as a basis if every vertex in $G \setminus B$ is uniquely identified by its distances to B, provided that all vertices in B are at least one step away from a specific given vertex $u$ (i.e., they are not neighbors of, or equal to, $u$). A mathematical model is developed to simulate the movement of water in porous materials, applicable to both groundwater flow and hydropower applications involving saturated plants. The existing method for determining pressure potential and fluid velocity in simplified cases is extended to address a broader range of conditions. Consequently, equations describing the pressure potential and fluid velocity are derived. Furthermore, a set of equations is derived to model the development of water table surfaces, specifically addressing scenarios where the water table's slope is significant. Finally, these model equations are utilized to formulate a set of differential equations designed to calculate the steady-state water table surface.

Flue gas desulfurization (FGD) systems are essential for minimizing SO₂ emissions from power plants. This study evaluates the efficacy of combining ozone injection with ultraviolet (UV) radiation to remove sulfur dioxide from flue gas. Research indicates that this combined ozone/UV approach offers a viableDesulfurization pathway characterized by high SO₂ removal rates and energy efficiency, utilizing relatively low O₃ concentrations while maintaining effective performance under a broad range of operational conditions.

Synaptic and neuron models are essential for simulating artificial neuromorphic networks, which is why their parameters must be easily adjustable. Moreover, to scale these architectures for large-scale use, a multi-level architectural description is required. This approach allows designers working at different abstraction levels to collaborate effectively without interfering with one another. We introduce an open-virtual framework based on the SystemC hardware design language to facilitate these needs. Written in C++, this virtual library provides standard building blocks for creating custom configurations. It supports various spike encoding schemes, diverse network topologies, and multiple strategies for weight management between neurons and synapses. By adopting an modular, hierarchical design, this system can be extended to include new neural models and to integrate with external tools, such as for computing network activation functions or performing online learning.

Decision-making under ambiguity is a central challenge in contemporary neural methods, particularly for image classification tasks that involve classes present only in marginal portions of the training data. A critical limitation of existing approaches is their tendency to output probabilistic estimates based on assumptions of independence across data samples, a strategy that often results in overconfidence that increases as the marginality of a class grows. This study addresses this deficiency by introducing the Indecision Forest (IDF) method, a new non-parametric ensemble technique tailored to mitigate such excessive confidence and accurately model ambiguity. Unlike traditional models, IDF explicitly simulates uncertainty by incorporating an indecision layer that blocks forward propagation when the output feature map falls below a specific threshold. The authors provide both the intuitive case reasoning behind IDF and a formal proof demonstrating that this architecture enables effective training via backpropagation despite the discontinuity caused by the indecision phase. Experimental evaluations within various settings of the ImageNet subset MNIST-70k reveal that running time has decreased while accuracy remains consistent with conventional models in dominant scenarios, all without incurring performance penalties.

Discrete Time Warping (DTW) is widely recognized as the standard method for measuring distance between time series. While the algorithm's flexibility allows it to align sequences of varying lengths distorted by noise or temporal shifts, this versatility results in high computational complexity. To address this computational burden, a new method called prunedDTW has been developed that dramatically reduces processing time. However, this optimization introduces a new constraint: the algorithm fails if the initial calculation at the first element is too computationally expensive. This paper introduces a strategy for proactively managing such risky starting nodes by establishing criteria to discard entire sequences of candidates early in the process. Designed to function correctly even when discarding the initial element, this approach enables the retrieval of significant similarities. Furthermore, we detail a two-phase system that lever this early discarding capability to similarly detect highly relevant matches.

This study aims to compare the relative effectiveness of inquiry-based and traditional detailed evaluation mechanisms for teaching software testing. Adopting a mixed-method approach, an empirical study was conducted involving 130 undergraduate participants across two distinct experimental conditions who performed six programming tasks requiring testing proficiency. While traditional methods utilized line and mutation coverage metrics alongside feedback on specific testing failures, the inquiry-based group received questions about test suite outcomes and options. The traditional group achieved significantly higher performance than the other group, though both produced bug-free code at comparable rates. Furthermore, the traditional group reported greater self-efficacy and enjoyment, while all participants found the inquiry-based task more demanding. These findings suggest that while the inquiry-based strategy supports the development of critical thinking skills, traditional evaluation mechanisms currently yield more effective overall instruction in software testing.

Explainable AI is a critical research domain, particularly as neural networks are increasingly deployed in high-stakes fields like healthcare and finance within current industry 4.0 applications. Since deep neural networks (DNNs) operate as black boxes, researchers are increasingly turning to post hoc interpretability methods. A notable challenge is the often limited human understanding of these models, which results in explanations filled with technical jargon that fail to be truly understandable. This study addresses this knowledge gap by leveraging termwo-colour analysis—a method revealing DNN concepts and anti-concepts—and integrating it with constraint-based inductive logic programming (ILP). We developed a novel ILP framework that generates more human-centric and linguistically robust definitions for the discovered network concepts. Empirical results on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets validate that our ILP-based definitions offer deeper insights into the internal logic of DNNs, outperforming conventional approaches by delivering more accurate, specific, and truthful predictions.

Over-complete full-color depth maps from the BAIR Robot Hand using a multi-layer Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) demonstrates significant model capacity, as it can learn non-linear representations effectively. However, research indicates that increasing this capacity to handle non-linearity may degrade performance by causing excessive smoothing of the predicted depth values. Blurring this depth excessively often obscures the fine structural details within the scene, thereby reducing the model's utility for tasks like motion estimation. To address these limitations, this study advocates integrating regularization techniques during training to preserve edge sharpness in the generated depth predictions. Specifically, we evaluate various Regularization-by-Example methods alongside a novel "depth deconvolution" layer. This layer functions as a learned inverse operation to the encoder, enabling the network to identify and correct any smoothing errors during the regression phase. Experimental results confirm that these enhancements allow GCNs to achieve greater representational capacity while producing sharper, higher-quality depth maps.

This study details a search for dark substance alongside a Z boson that decays into electrons or muons, conducted by the CMS experiment at CERN's Proton Synchrotron. Using the full dataset of 2016 with an integrated luminosity reaching 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, the analysis shows no evidence for new substance. Upper limits on the production cross section of one or more final state objects comprising significant missing transverse momentum and either a Z or an electron-plus-quark pair (electron-plus-jets) are established at the 95% confidence level. These constraints are determined within the framework of an effective field theory model. Cross section suppression extends the lowest-scale effective field theory operator from 10 TeV to 11.5 TeV (for the four-lepton operator) or 11 TeV (for an electron-plus-jets configuration) respectively.

By exploiting the inherent gauge invariance of the general correlators and the associated light-ray operators, we construct novel (quasi)parton distributions featuring both transverse momentum ($k_\perp$) and transverse localization ($\vec{b}_\perp$). Our findings indicate that this $k_\perp$-dependent structure encodes the transverse localization of partons within the hadron, a dependency made visible through a Collins-Moore-Soper (CMM) gauge transformation. This research focuses on modeling one-dimensional time series and more broadly, multi-dimensional sequential data that exhibit heavy tails but do not necessarily conform to stable distributions. We propose an iterative, unsupervised algorithm capable of jointly estimating the left skewness (or lack of skew) and sample size from data streams. The method relies on extracting sufficient statistics via Pareto graphs and a fitted Pareto graph, which are then used in an estimation phase through either classical or Bayesian frameworks. When dealing with multidimensional sequences, we introduce a technique to separate temporal correlations from the heavy-tailed marginal distributions. Our approach is validated using both synthetic datasets and real-world financial stock price records. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of this methodology in dynamically adjusting both the skewness and the window length of a sliding analysis period.

We investigate $\alpha$-attractor models featuring inflaton potentials that depend on both the radial and angular components of the Kähler metric. Specifically, we explore models where this function is either directly proportional to the squared radial coordinate or follows a power law involving such coordinate; the latter offers significantly greater flexibility. Because our model space is defined by an infinite set of parameters, we utilize forecast techniques to analyze these cases, applying the method to both model spaces with predictions for both model types. Finally, we conduct a detailed study of four selected models—two representing each functional category—to verify if they satisfy the necessary observational constraints.

In this study, we investigate individual behavior within sealed-bid auctions regarding the allocation of goods and revenues, utilizing a second-price auction framework where participants submit private valuations without knowledge of others' offers. The collected data reveals that while human valuations often deviate from theoretical equilibrium predictions—primarily exhibiting demands lower than modeled states, occasionally going negative, and sometimes showing positive variability—we conduct a simulation analysis to explore these anomalies. The proposed second-price auction model, anchored in the concept of trust, successfully replicates these irrational deviations. Specifically, trust acts as a decisive factor in explaining why agents might bid below their true willingness to pay or exhibit other non-equilibrium behaviors. The results indicate a robust consistency between a theory with endogenous trust and the observed experimental outcomes, underscoring the significant role trust plays in real-world auction participation.

Although often considered a linear phenomenological extension of teleparallel gravity $f(T)$, the new framework $f(Q)$ is a novel generalized formalism based on the non-metricity scalar $Q$. In the context of cosmology, this theory demonstrates significant potential for describing both inflation and dark energy phases. Focusing on a non-local rotational symmetric (LORS) Bianchi-I universe within $f(Q)$-gravity, we derive the governing dynamical equations. We subsequently analyze the evolution of these solutions to demonstrate that the $f(Q)$-based LORS Bianchi-I cosmological model indeed undergoes isotropization.

In this study, we present a collection of 921 high-quality neural artistic images categorized into 11 distinct classes, such as painting, photography, and graphic design. We introduce a robust classification framework that integrates both supervised and unsupervised methods, as well as a high-performance low-level image editing network capable of producing highly accurate classifiers. Furthermore, we establish the Neural Artist Evaluation (NAE) benchmark, which consists of 165 images and 10 NAE tasks ranging from image similarity detection to novelty identification. A comprehensive benchmarking experiment shows that the best existing methods improve by approximately 10% across all 10 NAF tasks. We also release our source code and image datasets at https://github.com/lylyzhang/Neural-Artistry.

We present a unified framework addressing the net loss of neutral kaon regeneration in the E791 experiment alongside the pseudoscalar and vector meson flavor anomalies observed in LHCb, Shopov, Belle, ATLAS, CMS, and CDF data, utilizing minimal interactions in a new composite sector with characteristic energy scale $T \sim \text{TeV}$. This model simultaneously enhances the ratios $\mathcal{B}(B \to J/\psi \phi)/\mathcal{B}(B^0_s \to J/\psi \phi)$ and $K_S/K_L$ from their Standard Model predictions. Specifically, it accounts for the anomalous neutral-kaon regeneration via the interference of a $K_S/K_L$ resonance arising from a composite diquark-lepton interaction $\bar{K}_L \to J/\psi \phi$, where the dominant contribution stems from a vector resonance exchange. Similarly, the anomalous ratio of anomalous decay rates is explained by off-diagonal $B_B$ and $B_B$ mixing amplitudes mediated primarily by heavy vector resonances. With a single set of model parameters, fit quality is significantly improved, yielding a best-fit scale of $T \approx 1.5^{+0.3}_{+00} \text{TeV}$. Additionally, we outline strategies for detecting this phenomenon at the High-Luminosity LHC and propose corresponding experimental signatures.

In an increasingly information-driven environment, information literacy has emerged as a critical competency. While literature confirms the importance of teaching this skill to university students, literature also indicates a scarcity of teaching materials supporting it. Since information literacy encompasses a broad scope, no single tool can effectively cover the entire domain; therefore, we propose a strategy for deriving such materials from academic articles. This paper introduces a methodology to extract information-seeking queries and their answers from these texts. Our approach represents an alternative to traditional Information Access Research methods—which focus on large-scale web or database collections—and demonstrates the feasibility of this extraction process through a concrete implementation. Ultimately, we aim to expand the repertoire of queries available to the community, thereby benefiting Natural Language Processing applications that rely on query-based training data.

Recent simulations by our group, involving rapid flavor conversions in the late stages of core-collapse within a 15 $M_{\odot}$ star, revealed that these instabilities persist even when hydrodynamic turbulence is accounted for. To isolate these effects, we ran additional 3D simulations with time-stationary lepton number profiles, ranging from low to high mass scales of neutrino density inhomogeneities. Our results indicate that while this turbulence amplifies both spiral and sheet-type instability amplitudes, it does not alter their fundamental characteristics. Specifically, typical conversion volumes remain modest, staying well below 10 cm$^3$, which is insufficient to significantly impact the neutrino signal output.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) remains a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition among children, yet current diagnostic methods rely on subjective behavioral observations and the interpretation of fMRI data, which often lack precision. To address this, we proposed a deep learning framework to bolster the diagnosis of ADHD by identifying significant regions within the brain. The protocol involved three key stages: (1) filtering out non-informative voxels to concentrate on crucial areas; (2) extracting features using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to train a secondary network for diagnosis; and (3) fine-tuning the CNN by optimizing the binary classification accuracy of the CNN. The outcome demonstrates that this approach successfully pinpointed essential regions relevant to ADHD status and leveraged their features to enhance the overall diagnostic accuracy.

The proposed Dist-time SISI model distinguishes itself by allowing a unique infection and recovery process for each pathogen, allowing recovered individuals to potentially succumb to subsequent infections. In addition to standard Susceptible, Infectious, and Susceptible states, this framework includes specific "Infection 1" and "Recovery 1" and "Infection 2 and Re-covery 2" states to track the progression through two distinct diseases, where transitions utilize separate transmission and recovery rates for each disease. We establish a master equation for this Dist-time SISI model and analyze its equilibrium distribution by leveraging a corresponding Markov chain; findings indicate ergodicity when the diseases do not cross-infect, while an intricate coexistence of infections requires altered, cross-infective parameters. Our numerical explorations of this system's state space demonstrate that when mutual cross-infectivity exists, the total number of currently infectious individuals serves as a reliable predictor for which virus is currently more prevalent in terms of total patient counts.

Acronyms are ubiquitous in technical writing, frequently appearing multiple times within a single document. Given the ease with which auto-dictionary systems can locate established meanings for common terms, distinct disambiguation algorithms typically handle the identification of different variations. However, the repetition rate of those acronyms diminishes in less common contexts, often failing to reach the frequency thresholds required to trigger automatic processing. Additionally, context-based disambiguation algorithms are generally sensitive to domain shifts, which can cause a significant decline in accuracy when applied across different specialized fields. To address these limitations, the MadDog project introduces a system designed to identify acronyms within domain-specific texts and link instances of the same acronym to existing entries in an acronym dictionary maintained by the project. The algorithm underpinning MadDog was developed specifically to function independently of the data volume associated with acronyms and without reliance on training data from the target domain. This study details the algorithm and its performance through an analysis involving three distinct acronym sets drawn from the architecture, biology, and electronics sectors. Empirical results indicate that while the algorithm's precision and recall are generally robust, its performance is most pronounced when applied to electronic texts.

This study introduces a fresh mechanism for directional switching of charge and energy currents alongside a newly devised architecture for thermal diode operations, both grounded in quantum Hall (QH) edge states at the integer QH effect plateau $\nu = 2$. The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) framework serves as a global standard for structuring clinical diagnoses. To address noise in tomographic acquisitions, iterative inverse problem methodologies are utilized, where the goal is to estimate object properties from measured data. Bayesian inference has emerged as a significant approach within this domain, capable of estimating not only the object but also its associated uncertainty. Nevertheless, simulation-based techniques based on Bayes theorem demand the repeated execution of a forward model, rendering them prohibitive when this model is simulation-based and computationally expensive. To overcome these limitations, this work introduces an original, analytical, and differential method for efficiently calculating forward model uncertainties. We validate and illustrate the utility of this method through applications to arrays of phase oscillators as well as intrinsically diverse self-oscillators.

Specifically, applications of "semantictic" or meaning-based computing to the domain of image analysis have emerged but remain largely underutilized. In industrial gas-solid stationary beds, such as those found in chemical or pharmaceutical manufacturing, the complex, non-uniform distribution of temperature is recognized as a critical factor influencing the overall reaction selectivity. However, obtaining experimental data on local heat profiles within such reactors remains exceptionally difficult. This study successfully combines pulsed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with numerical simulations to investigate and validate the three-dimensional heat distribution in a lab-scale fixed-bed reactor. The experiment utilized a diamagnetic tracer suspended in the bed, through which water was pumped to establish a defined convective heat transfer current. By leveraging the narrow point-spread function of the MRI system along with an optimized low-temperature range in the pulse sequence, the study achieved precise spatial and thermal resolution. These high-fidelity measurements were then compared against numerical simulations performed with a validated macroscopic model, confirming the capability of MRI as an advanced tool for validating heat and mass transport models in gas-solid stationary beds.

Biomolecular condensates, which form via liquid-liquid phase separation within the cellular cytoplasm and nucleoli, function as essential, highly concentrated microcompartment for organizing cellular components. In eukaryotic cells, these structures appear to self-assemble without direct external guidance, a process potentially complicated by the lack of precise control over size and the risk of uncontrolled co-assembly of molecules that need spatial separation. This study investigates these challenges using a computational model of a cell containing two condensates sharing some, but not all, constituent proteins. The researchers found that a limited set of six proteins can reliably generate distinct phase boundary conditions, effectively preventing the common proteins from mislocalizing to the wrong condensate or causing system collapse. Notably, these proteins strongly interact with each other and exhibit only weak self-affinity. This configuration aligns with current biological observations and supports a model where the robustness of cellular organization relies on mutual, indirect interactions among molecules rather than strong, individual binding events alone, confirming that condensates can successfully utilize shared components to maintain a stable configuration.

Accurate and computationally efficient simulation of cardiac mechanics relies on a robust spatial discretization strategy, necessitating the conditional numbering of the Finite Element Method's stiffness system of linear equations. These equations feature a sparse, symmetric, and positive-definite structure, which we analyze using the two-level and fully two-level hierarchical Búscalo (H-B) algorithms, along with their fully two-level variants (Full H-B). Assisting this analysis, we developed a comparison tool to examine the spectral characteristics, cluster distribution, and eigenvector patterns of the condensed operators. Findings indicate critical spectral and topological differences among these four solvers, leading to practical outcomes where fully two-level algorithms demonstrate a consistent, substantial advantage in solving equations arising from mechanical heart simulations compared to their two-level counterparts.

Social tagging systems have established a legacy of supporting diverse social functionalities unique to the web 2.0 ecosystem. Using the Automated Text Analysis (AutoTS) technique to examine more than 25,000 tags attached to more than 10,000 items across ten prominent platforms (such as Del.icio.us, StumbleUpon, and Flickr), our research reveals that user activity remains highly temporal. We observe that tags are frequently applied repeatedly in short bursts and removed shortly after. Despite the ability of technologies to manage this inherent volatility, there is a notable absence of scholarly attention on this characteristic. We also identify two forms of collaboration: interest exchange and tag reuse. While collaboration in system design primarily targets tag reuse, most user activity actually involves interest exchange. We propose that co-occurrence and correlation analyses—rooted in Bayesian and Borda theories—can be utilized to distinguish interest exchange from reuse. This capability enables more refined modeling of user behavior, which is essential for creating effective tools that support both forms of collaboration and other core web 2.0 functions.

The emergence of acoustic metagratings at microwave frequencies has sparked significant interest in their remarkable manipulation capabilities. Nevertheless, realizing these structures at higher frequencies remains challenging due to inherent fabrication limitations, which hinder the creation of features small enough to generate forces effective against momentum transfer to a diffraction grating operating at visible light levels. To overcome fabrication barriers, this study demonstrates the diffraction produced by a metagrating engineered for the near-infrared regime, where wavelengths exceed 1000 nm. The demonstrated device was fabricated using two-photon lithography, a technique capable of sculpting three-dimensional architectures with sub-100 nm precision. Through both experimental validation and theoretical modeling, we confirm the metagrating's diffusion properties align with predictions, successfully diffusing a collimated beam into the first three diffraction orders.

This work introduces global robust solutions for the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model that exhibit significant extensive time behavior. Initially, utilizing compactness arguments, we establish the existence of global robust solutions defined over an unlimited time interval \([0, +\infty)\). Subsequently, under specific constraints, a unique global robust solution is defined. Finally, under additional assumptions, we prove that this solution converges to a standard (classical) solution.

The concept of the Integrated Access Backhaul (IAB) was initially conceived within 5G New Radio (5G NR) to enable a base station to utilize the same frequency band for serving user equipment and transmitting backhaul data. Although the initial framework addresses only wireline links, extending support to mobile networks would significantly enhance deployment flexibility. Adopting mobile IAB empowers both user-centric access points and the core of this architecture with high mobility. While advantageous, mobile IAB introduces complexities regarding synchronization, interference mitigation, and robust management that must be overcome. Consequently, overcoming these barriers is essential for broadening the base station coverage footprint. This review paper provides a thorough overview of the conventional wire-centric access backhaul system, outlines the benefits and risks associated with mobilizing IAB, highlights current academic research into mobile implementations, and presents open issues along with potential development trajectories and future directions for further investigation.

This paper addresses the issue of optimizing control parameters for feature selection within evolutionary algorithms (CAs), a process that is frequently executed in an ad-hoc manner. To shift toward a more objective approach, we propose a novel methodology grounded in global sensitivity analysis (GSA). This framework leverages the variance-based GSA metric, specifically the Shapley variance decomposition (SWDE), to quantify how control parameters influence the algorithm's performance (measured by F1-score) and its effectiveness (measured as the percentage of irredundant relevant features identified). By minimizing the latter, our strategy seeks to enhance both performance and efficiency, while the former is improved through the optimization of the CA-based feature selection process.

Our experimental design, conducted on the well-established WSDE, comprehensively varies the parameters of the CA to calculate these sensitivity measures and the performance metrics across a range of datasets. Finally, this methodology is demonstrated through a case study applying the algorithm to identify features for classifying PPS and NPPS cases within the medical context of sleep disorders.

This paper explores several aspects of the wave equation derived from the dynamics of de Broglie waves within quantum mechanics. The wave equation for a free particle featuring constant mass is established by invoking the de Broglie wave formula alongside Einstein's mass-energy equivalence. Subsequently, the spatial components corresponding to Poynting vectors and probability current densities are derived for the wave equations representing both photons and massive particles, respectively. Finally, the similarities and distinctions among the respective electromagnetic waves, wave equations, Poynting vectors, and probability current densities of particles are analyzed.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) methods typically treat tasks as one-off opportunities, assuming a prior model or task-specific policy that discloses task knowledge when it begins. These limitations ignore two key aspects of how real-world agents operate: their persistent nature and their ability to accumulate cross-task experience. Although some RL approaches have started to address this issue, there is no standard benchmark to begin evaluating an agent's capabilities in this area. We introduce L2Explorer, a new simulation based on two-dimensional video games for assessing lifetime learning in RL agents. Our results compare five leading algorithms across three well-known titles, showing that L2Explorer supports diverse difficulty curves and can scale effectively with varying complexity levels.

The Lander Instrumentation and Data Acquisition and Systems Engineering (LIGER) project at Keck Observatory aims to create a novel 2.5D, three-dimensional, and spectropolarimetric camera capable of uncovering connections in stellar activity across various scales and times. To achieve comprehensive coverage of stellar magnetic fields, this ambitious initiative employs two distinct instruments simultaneously: one targeting magnetograph spectro-polarimetry (SP) at a resolution of 0.02 Å (R = 100,000), and another covering wide-field magnetography (WFM) from 0.2 to 1.0 nm (R = 20,000). Both modes utilize LIGER's dual-channel architecture, which measures circular and linear polarization independently. This engineering feat involves combining two separate Spectrometer and Control Units (SCUs) and merging their data streams. As the project entered its critical testing phase at Keck in early 2019, WFM SCUs were deployed first, followed by SP SCUs later that year. This installation triggered the deployment of the Data Acquisition and Control System (DACOS), a critical component responsible for managing the instrument's electronics, power distribution, and optical paths while handling the collection, transfer, and processing of scientific data. The following discussion outlines the DACOS design and its operational framework, emphasizing the data management infrastructure necessary to support LIGER's scientific objectives.

This study examines planar, unbounded 2D symmetric (up to mirror reflection) steady states within the Euler framework by analyzing the flow of the wave operator associated with linearized perturbations around these states. The identified base flows correspond to simple shear flows characterized by linear velocity profiles. The findings also reveal that for magnitudes of the vorticity gradient exceeding a critical value ($\nu > 1$), the migration direction flips, aligning with predictions from the Kelvin-Helmholtz zoom-in analysis. These results are consistent with the scaling laws derived from the Kelvin-Helmholtz zoom-in analysis.

We introduce three classes of deterministic partial differential equations that correspond to the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation via the Hopf-Cole transformation. These models feature nonlocal terms representing "effective slopes," designed to correct the gradient in regions of high gradient while preserving the integrability of solution exponentials. A key result demonstrates that the regularity of the associated KPZ surfaces improves significantly compared to standard KPZ formulations, rising from $C^{1/2-\epsilon}$ to $C^{1-\epsilon}$ or even $C^\infty$ and real-analytic classes. These models maintain a nonlinearity strong enough to prevent linearization methods and allow for singular nonlinear analysis where the effective potential remains smoother than the nonlinearity itself. Consequently, the analysis relies primarily on this smoother potential rather than the rougher nonlinearity. Our methodology draws upon techniques previously applied to singular perturbations and smooth perturbation theories.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has drastically altered global society and public health strategies, necessitating prompt decisions regarding testing allocation, contact tracing, and healthcare resource management to mitigate harm. While optimal decision-making typically relies on robust statistical models backed by reliable data, the scarcity of information in many regions—especially within the early stages of outbreaks—often forces these data dependencies to fall apart. In this context, we introduce a methodology designed to derive actionable insights for pandemic response by leveraging data sources that others might overlook or ignore. We test this approach using South Africa, examining how varying assumptions about data reliability influence policy outcomes. Our work uses Levene statistics for hypothesis testing to assess whether means and variances from variant datasets come from a common distribution. Leaning on LE tests, we show that reliable data can effectively guide policy, even when mixed with unreliable data that may lead to false positives in hypothesis testing. We further demonstrate that our strategy for incorporating unreliable data produces outcomes nearly identical to those using only valid data.

An additive theorem developed to improve upon Freiman's finding from 2006. This research presents a result enhancing Freiman's $3k\text{-}4$ theorem. Specifically, if $A$ is a finite subset within an abelian group with a size of at least 7 and a doubling factor where $|A+A| \leq 3k\text{-}4$, then there exists an arithmetic progression $AP$ containing $A$ such that this proportion satisfies the stricter bounds of $\text{Proportion} \leq 20\text{k}\text{-}12$. This thesis also addresses several open questions concerning the optimal constants associated with an arithmetic progression containing such sets $A$, as well as extends the result to cases involving non-empty subsets.

Deep learning has proven highly effective in classifying diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma by analyzing the retinal fundus images of both healthy individuals and those with disease. This success stems from the comprehensive information contained within these images, which allows models to capture intricate pathological features. While this facilitates accurate categorization, it is worth noting that individuals with glaucoma may exhibit no visible signs in fundus images, offering no clear pathology for the algorithm to detect. To fully leverage detectable pathological features for glaucoma detection, we propose a novel image synthesis technique that combines two key inputs: 50-degree OCT scans and patient demographic information. By integrating OCT data with OCT-GU data, which stands for "Ocuplt-Gravure Unit Data" derived from "Cup-to-Disc Ratio" and "Glaucoma-Heim-Hertel Visual Field" and "Glaucoma-Histological Grading Using Fundus Analysis," the resulting enhanced multimodal dataset allows us to effectively utilize this information for two-stage image synthesis. This two-stage framework first involves finding relevant parts of each image using cross-attention to create an initial representation, which is then used to synthesize new images through a diffusion process. The resulting images offer a comprehensive view of both diseases, leading to improved categorization accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that this synthetic approach enhances the accuracy of our proposed system.

This paper explores a methodology to analyze how ICU admissions influence the chest X-ray appearances of COVID-19 patients. While the broader landscape of these patients' ICU admissions remains somewhat elusive, these symptoms may hold significant implications for enhancing diagnostic accuracy through AI-driven image analysis. We hypothesize that such symptoms could be better understood by applying time-series analysis techniques to X-ray data acquired at different time intervals. Consequently, we anticipate that the gradual changes associated with ICU admission will become more apparent through the use of time-series prediction to forecast the progression of COVID-19 cases in ICU settings.

This study examines how light propagates through spherically layered transparent media, focusing on the identification of transmission eigenvalues and their associated functions. The analysis begins by deriving the expressions for the transmission eigenvalue boundaries, thereby restricting the search domain for these eigenvalues. Furthermore, a dedicated method is introduced to identify the boundaries of the transmission eigenfunctions, both inside the sphere and within the external material. With this tool, a step-by-step algorithm is established to relocate all transmission eigenvalue-function pairs using an iterative approach. The validity and effectiveness of both the proposed method and algorithm are confirmed by applying them to sequentially layered spheres composed of dielectric or optically active dielectric substances.

Intent exploration is a crucial component of dialogue understanding, which is especially vital for new product launches or existing services that accumulate numerous unknown intent categories over time. Traditional approaches typically depend on a vast assembly of annotated instances to achieve satisfactory performance, often necessitating costly and laborious retraining efforts whenever a service updates its intent categories. In contrast, this paper introduces **PEtENT** (**P**re-training **Et**e**NT**), a novel large-scale pre-trained model designed to overcome these challenges while facilitating new intent learning. We achieve this by leveraging a hierarchical cross-attention mechanism to merge word-level token embeddings with intent-level semantic representations derived from background knowledge. Our proposed training objective harnesses contrastive learning to strengthen the alignment between word and intent embeddings while simultaneously pushing disparate samples apart. Extensive evaluations across three public datasets and a real-world scenario demonstrate that PEtENT attains state-of-the-art results under both full training and few-shot learning conditions. Furthermore, our solutions have been deployed and integrated into Alibaba's official customer support system.

This study utilizes historical data to reassess Leggett's (1997) analysis of the performance of the Absahl-Bauer-Sutherland (ABS) hydrogen viscosity formula. Our findings indicate that despite significant improvements suggested by these new simulations, the ABS model remains inferior to models developed by more recent studies. Specifically, models based on the Lennard-Jones 12-6 model by Chapman and Enock, as well as the hydrogen-specific model from Naudet et al. are superior to ABS in predicting viscosity. While an accurate potential function allows for highly precise predictions of transport properties via simulation—as demonstrated by Naudet et al.—viscosity can also be estimated with high accuracy using simple empirical formulas, such as the one proposed by安德森 (Anderson).

Identifying interactions between objects in complex scenes is an increasingly vital challenge in visual analysis, as this capability supports higher-level visual reasoning tasks. While recent advancements have largely concentrated on minimizing false negatives, this study focuses specifically on addressing erroneous detections (EPs). We observe that a substantial portion of EPs stems from the dual encoding of visual relations, and the frequency of such duplicate detections correlates positively with the total count of pairs identified by a model. The core mechanism behind these duplicate pairs is the presence of ambiguous visual properties that allow multiple valid relationship interpretations. Consequently, we introduce a novel detection framework leveraging ambiguity awareness to mitigate the prevalence of EPs. First, we establish a new benchmark limited to non-redundant relation instances across current state-of-the-art datasets to better evaluate strategies for eliminating duplicates. Second, leveraging this dataset, we propose an epistemic uncertainty-based module designed to identify and flag duplicate relations by highlighting areas of high predictive ambiguity. Finally, we incorporate a confidence-boosting module that enhances the model's certainty when generating novel visual relationships. Extensive experiments conducted on the COCO and VisualRelations datasets confirm that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance specifically in the reduction of erroneous positives.

Quantum entropies derived from entropy operators serve as potent tools within the realm of large-scale quantum states and operations. This study defines the notion of "computation using entropic distance," enabling calculations regarding optimal quantum communication costs associated with specific operations in both composite and tripartite systems. As an initial application, the paper defines measurement relative to entropic distance and applies this framework to analyze the connection cost linked to quantum states resulting from the action of entropic-distant feasible measurements. To illustrate the approach, the analysis examines connection costs for states formed via the Teliowekfeble measurement method, an approach utilized in entropy stabilization procedures.

This study presents a full architecture designed to construct social relationship graphs by predicting social attributes within a given context, focusing on key traits like the relation's direction, distance, and the nature of the interaction. Unlike previous approaches where these directionality metrics were handled independently or as unified but flawed standards, this work integrates all tasks into a single network. The paper highlights how a unified method outperforms baseline models, offering greater efficiency through multi-task learning while maintaining or enhancing overall accuracy in the majority of tasks. Additionally, the framework demonstrates strong generalization capabilities, allowing it to perform effectively on unseen image datasets.

While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved success in many image recognition tasks, they often require extensive layers and parameters, leading to challenges in efficiency and speed. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Active Graph Message Transfer Networks (AGMTN), a novel framework for visual recognition designed to drastically cut down network complexity. This approach models visual processing as an active inference task where information flow is controlled by a selective mechanism. Unlike current methods that lose features passively through operations like batch normalization, pooling, and channel-wise convolution, AGMTN enables the network to actively seek specific features. By partitioning layers into localized subnetworks and implementing this selective information flow, we achieve a more streamlined architecture capable of superior efficiency and velocity. Experimental results on various tasks, including classification, detection, and semantic segmentation, confirm the effectiveness of this method, demonstrating performance improvements with up to a 40% reduction in layers and parameters.

By selecting the digits based on these binary coefficients to minimize the count of adders required by any constant factor, the architecture maximizes operational speed and minimizes area, thereby achieving the smallest possible logic synthesis results. Mathematical analysis and comparative data validate the approach, demonstrating its superior performance in both synthesis efficiency and processing speed.

Deep learning's recent surge in popularity is largely credited to its remarkable success, yet high energy consumption and extensive computational requirements have hindered its deployment in resource-constrained environments. Drawing inspiration from the human brain, which features an intricate network of interconnected neurons capable of learning and performing diverse functions efficiently, the field of Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) has gained significant traction as a potential solution. By leveraging fundamental quantum principles like superposition and entanglement, QNNs offer a powerful framework for pattern recognition and machine learning tasks. This review article provides a concise overview of their operational principles and existing applications. Furthermore, it critically examines the primary obstacles that must be overcome to achieve practical, large-scale implementations of these networks.

The primary goal of semantic segmentation is to classify every pixel into specific categories. While this approach holds immense promise for the autonomous driving industry, it remains constrained by limited performance when processing regions with sparse textural details or significant viewpoint variations. Although hyperspectral images (HIs) have become a standard for such challenges due to their ability to capture rich spectral data across numerous bands, they are rarely collected in complex urban environments because of high acquisition costs and low data efficiency. However, multi-band satellite data, which offers a cost-effective spectral profile similar to that of HIs, presents a viable alternative for enhancing the capabilities of pixel-level semantic analysis. This study proposes a lightweight, spectral-hypersite joint representation framework utilizing hyperspectral data to facilitate more accurate segmentation in extensive cityscapes. By extracting both spectral characteristics and spatial layout information, which are then fused through a convolutional layer to generate a comprehensive representation, the model effectively captures distinct visual properties of various objects. Furthermore, the framework includes a spectral-hypersite attention module to refine feature details while maintaining gradient flow via direct backpropagation. This design ensures stable optimization of the network without compromising training efficiency, all demonstrated through validation on the COCO dataset.

We investigate the intermediate phase between star-accretion and TDEs using numerical simulations that treat the dynamics of a tidal sphere surrounding the black hole. We examine a range of parameters governing these systems to derive power-law distributions of tidal disruption events, observing that the resulting slopes align well with empirical data from actual TDEs. Additionally, the specific dependence of these events on the black hole's spin indicates that an intermediate-mass black hole could ingest a star entirely, provided it begins at roughly 10 times the spin of its counterpart, aligning it with observations.

We aim to enhance session-based recommendations through deep learning using the Co-trainer (CoTr) of two or more underfitted sub-models on distinct but related tasks. To achieve this, we introduce a novel architecture, self-guided text-subgraph recommendation (SG-TSG), which combines user-item sequences with session-text-subgraph data. Our framework consists of SG-TSG and SG-GBL, two underfitted models that work in tandem on parallel yet correlated tasks to refine one another, with specific random dropout applied to each during training. To resolve data scarcity caused by filtering, we employ a fusion technique that merges the main task with auxiliary SG-TSG tasks, and to tackle potential domain shift and concept drift between these tasks, we develop the method of self-guided text-subgraph augmentation (SG-TSG). This scenario replaces discrete internal fibration groups with non-commutative algebra of functions, which can be approximated by discrete internal fibration groups in the infrared regime while retaining significant implications in the ultraviolet regime. We introduce a technique called boundary transient-current method (BT-CNM) involving two-photon absorption to map charge transport in diamond crystals. This approach generates an electric field within the material via a focused visible pulsed laser, producing excitations within a specific depth-resolved volume determined by the non-linear absorption's characteristic depth. Simultaneously, ultrafast voltage pulses trigger another field within the diamond, generating flow of mobile charge carriers. By measuring the resulting currents at the surface, this process maps the movement of charges along three dimensions. This versatile method allows for adjusting the mapping volume's spatial scale from micrometers to nanometers by modifying the voltage pulse's intensity and duration, and it can pinpoint where in the crystal the carriers are transported. Validation of the BT-CNM involving voltages and pulses in synthetic single crystal diamond was conducted, with the technique's accuracy confirmed against established results from electrical measurements and Time-Resolved Photoconductive Gating (TRPCG). As this method maps the movement of charges within the material under fields, it has significant implications for understanding the performance of diamond in high-speed digital devices and quantum technologies.

Our results show that a multi-classification strategy generally outperforms single-class approaches. Furthermore, a two-step process that separates detection from classification yielded better accuracy than attempting to handle both tasks simultaneously on non-hypotetical data.

This study investigates the preservation of stability and safety in feedback control loops in the face of adversarial disturbances. While existing literature primarily focuses on reconstructing disturbance signals or developing robust optimization policies tailored for specific threats, this work introduces a less constrained policy search approach. This new method relies on learning probabilistic models of the plant while accounting for both non-stochastic uncertainties and adversarial attacks. By employing a model-driven policy search for probabilistic systems, this approach ensures robustness and adaptability to targets not pre-specified beforehand. Simulation results validate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy in achieving the desired performance objectives under conditions involving significant uncertainties and malicious disturbances.

Secure control remains a critical challenge in robotics, where ensuring that a manipulator avoids colliding with dynamic obstacles while completing its task is essential. Although Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers robust theoretical collision guarantees, its high computational cost renders it unsuitable for real-time deployment on mobile robotic platforms. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a configuration-aware secure control framework tailored for mobile robots. Rather than addressing collisions within a single task space, we reformulate the problem by simultaneously planning the robot's base trajectory and the space manipulator's joint trajectories in configuration space, ensuring collision-free operation. By leveraging a specific transformation in configuration space that maps collision constraints into bounds for the manipulator's joint velocities, we derive a novel, sufficiently slow-varying signal. This signal satisfies Control Barrier Function (CBF) conditions to enforce safety. Finally, we minimize the deviation between the system's actual trajectory and this reference slow-varying signal using an outer-loop CBF, thereby achieving real-time-safe control. Simulation outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

Natural language processing has given rise to numerous algorithmic approaches to summarization over the last twenty years. Among these are algorithms designed to achieve optimal text condensation by maximally preserving the original meaning. Although many non-extractive strategies have been developed, this paper focuses solely on extractive algorithms, which select sub-sequences from the source text to form the summary. We introduce a new extractive method that constructs a graph representation of sentence overlap to evaluate the distance between adjacent sentences based on their shared phrases and grammatical features. A new algorithmic technique is applied to traverse this sentence graph to identify an optimal path that remains within a specified threshold of graph distance, ensuring the selection of syntactically similar sentences. An effective method for estimating sentence vector distances is also established. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed algorithm outperforms existing baselines, including other extractive approaches and standard language models, across all evaluated metrics for English and Spanish news articles.

We introduce a novel architecture for a Bose-Einstein condensate (BECK)-based device, which functions as a switchable waveguide capable of a zero-to-two speed-of-light transition. By manipulating the Rabi frequency and detuning of an external laser field, the system's linear transport and non-linear self-focusing properties become fully controllable. Analysis of both regimes (paraxial and non-dispersive) reveals that this device supports distinct operations as a true switch, an amplifier, and a logic gate, all governed by the interplay between linear characteristics and non-linear phase shifts. Notably, while the amplification process inherently relies on quantum stochastic laser pumping, it proves to be an efficient mechanism for single photons. Finally, we observe that, under specific conditions, this logic operational mode supports operations using only classical signals, demonstrating that classical logic functions within the device do not necessitate the presence of any stochastic elements.

Determining the number of solutions and locating those answers remains the fundamental challenge in solving systems of multivariate polynomials. Although the degree of such polynomial equations can theoretically be arbitrarily high, existing state-of-the-art algorithms for computing the full spectrum of polynomial solutions often fail when confronted with high dimensions, particularly when the total degree is large or the number of variables significantly exceeds the count required for the dimensionality of the solution space's underlying variety. To overcome these computational hurdles, we present the algorithm ANSL (Algorithm for Computing Nontrivial Solutions Locus), which is specifically designed to determine only the non-trivial solution subset within a high-degree polynomial system. Our algorithm leverages existing methods to determine the total count of solutions and isolates those that are non-zero in count to within an $\epsilon$-precision box-norm. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that ANSL successfully identifies the nontrivial solution sets in the tested environments and delivers a speedup factor of up to 1000 times compared to conventional algorithms that attempt to compute all solutions.

High-energy shock waves produced by exploding stars in the Milky Way power synchrotron radiation from radio to gamma-rays, interacting with the dense interstellar medium to form observable large-scale emission structures. Semantic communications offer a mechanism to reduce transmission costs in next-generation wireless networks by sending only the essential information content rather than raw data. However, in environments characterized by high noise and scarce bandwidth, ensuring reliable communication remains difficult. This research introduces an innovative framework that integrates neuro-symbolic causal inference with signaling games to create more robust and dependable transfers under constrained bandwidth. The proposed signaling game enables the source to decompose meaning into semantic elements (the symbols) and tailor their encoding based on a specific communication goal (the logic). Specifically, we employ a combined inductive reasoning and machine learning approach at the receiver to identify both the underlying causal structures and the sender's strategic logic. By utilizing inductive reasoning, we allow the system to infer the rules for a particular task without retraining when switching contexts, while simultaneous learning ensures the encoder and decoder strategies evolve optimally for current channel conditions. Simulation outcomes confirm that the neuro-symbolic based strategy surpasses conventional high-redundancy methods, offering superior performance in terms of lower bitrates, enhanced resilience, and greater efficiency.

Predicting new terms between a pair of words remains an open challenge in Natural Language Processing. While existing systems often leverage word embeddings for this task, they frequently fail to incorporate the nuanced structure found in specific domain vocabularies. To address this, we present an improved hybrid model for predicting new term instances given two source terms. This framework integrates the Naive Bayes algorithm to analyze the explicit textual relationships within domain-specific datasets, simultaneously injecting latent knowledge derived from the implicit syntactic and semantic connections of general-purpose dictionaries and encyclopedic resources. Experiments running on both low and high dimensionality datasets indicate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art benchmarks when evaluating recall rates against established methods.

Session-based recommendation focuses on predicting the next item by extracting sessions from user behavior data, where a session represents a brief period of user activity. Current research predominantly utilizes recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to capture session features but often neglects the inherent structure and priority ordering inherent in user actions. This paper introduces a new CRR-based approach, which utilizes a graph neural network to represent sessions as graphs where items are nodes and edges represent interactions; the edge weights reflect interaction intensity. This method phases suggestions into two stages: (1) constructing an unbiased candidate set by identifying items that significantly increase the session graph representation, filtered via minimum ratio testing; (only then) (2) applying the unbiased set to generate recommendations based on predicted scores. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets confirm that this proposed system outperforms both baseline models and state-of-the-art techniques.

Active particles, such as colloids driven by an energy source, are able to self-propel by converting energy into mechanical work. Furthermore, we derived a theoretical framework based on a generalized Stokesian hydrodynamic formalism to explain these mechanisms. This theory accurately models the observed phenomena by extending active matter theory to systems with heterogeneous properties, specifically accounting for local variations in particle activity and passivity. Our findings provide crucial insights into how spatially controlled particle activity can be utilized for advanced manipulation techniques in microscopic environments.

To address variable signal blockages in vehicular networks caused by dynamic traffic interactions, we introduce a two-tier architecture integrating vehicles and Roadside Units (RSUs). Vehicles equipped with active antennas serve as relays within this framework, enabling dual transmission paths: directly from RSUs and alternatively via relay. By constructing an interference-aware network graph, we determine the relay policy necessary to maximize end-to-end secrecy capacity. Subsequently, we analyze key performance metrics, including average secrecy capacity, outage probability, and average end-to-end mean square error. Finally, simulation results reveal that utilizing relays enhances the average secrecy capacity of the 2-tier system. Notably, an optimal average secrecy capacity is achieved when relays possess active, rather than passive, capabilities.

Wikimedia Foundation's Wikipedia stands as one of the globe's most extensive encyclopedic resources, characterized by its community-driven editing model that enables both content creation and maintenance simultaneously. Owing to its foundational design, however, the platform frequently encounters the intrusion of inappropriate entries, such as advertising, pornography, or off-topic material, necessitating their identification and removal. Although professional staff work diligently to eliminate such content, persistent incidents occur, causing these inaccuracies to accumulate rapidly. Concurrently, ongoing enhancements in artificial intelligence have spurred increased adoption of machine learning techniques across content classification tasks. Capitalizing on the rich dataset inherent in Wikipedia—specifically its detailed user records which capture every edit alongside associated actions—the study analyzes patterns in contributor behaviors to train a trained Regressive Model. This model effectively regresses content sections by assigning "tagged sections" (e.g., infoboxes, lead-in paragraphs, and table-of-contents) based on the input data. By leveraging patterns in how professional staff tag poor-quality articles, the algorithm replicates this logic to identify inaccurate content automatically. Ultimately, while these methods offer a robust alternative or supplement to manual supervision for article quality control, the authors also acknowledge the necessity of integrating human oversight into a cohesive management framework.

Deep learning models are increasingly vital for modern AI systems, yet their extensive model parameters create barriers to deployment in resource-constrained settings, necessitating effective knowledge transfer to smaller architectures. Traditionally, evaluating a model's transferability to a target architecture requires training its target version with various downstream tasks. This study introduces a novel, lightweight, source-network centric approach called "infinite transferability evaluation." It assesses how transferable an source network is to a black-box target without requiring the target to be trained on specific tasks. The core mechanism involves a generative model that simulates functional similarities using similarity metrics between feature maps from source and target structures. This allows the source network to be evaluated against synthetically designed probe networks designed to capture distinct representational traits of the target. The authors argue this method provides an accurate and reliable prediction of transferability without the usual computational overhead. Empirical results indicate this new approach not only rivals but in some cases surpasses existing methods in correlating with true transfer performance across standard image classification benchmarks, all while avoiding the training of the target network.

Monocular depth estimation significantly influences the accuracy of force control within force-sensitive operations. However, because of the inherent depth ambiguity present in unmarked robot cameras, calculated depth values often deviate from the true geometry along a vertical scaling factor. Although previous studies addressed this specific issue, most depended on expert annotations to generate calibration datasets for their solutions. This study introduces an unsupervised framework that simultaneously fine-tunes both the depth scaling factor and the 6-DoF orientation of the end effector during image-based task execution. The model integrates a pre-trained depth encoder with two key components: a differentiable pose estimator, capable of deriving 6-DoF orientations from depth maps, and a regression module for estimating the vertical scaling factor. Rather than relying on ground-truth labels, our method utilizes unsupervised loss functions derived from task execution to align the estimated depth scaling factor and 6-DoF pose simultaneously with the actual physical reality, effectively correcting the scale distortion in the depth output. Validation was conducted on two synthetic environments and one real-world application, demonstrating superior performance over prior baselines.

The Low Resolution Laser Guided Telescope for Survey (LAMOST) is an innovative facility featuring a unique double optical system. The K-band channel utilizes 18 CCD detectors, each measuring $2048 \times 2048$ pixels, to simultaneously capture low-resolution spectra and a 2D photographic plate. Leveraging this capability, we have conducted time-domain surveys targeting variable stars. Derived from four consecutive K-band plates, our data encompass 1,010,627 stars, monitored for three nights with approximately 10-second intervals. The resulting light curves for these objects reveal diverse variability patterns, including eclipsing binary systems, pulsating variables, eruptive stars, single stars exhibiting outbursts, and out-of-eclipses binaries. The sample comprises 1,008 binary systems identified as eclipsing; among these, 1,004 cases display primary eclipses of total nature. Among the variable populations, dwarf novae are predominantly located in the galactic plane and exhibit characteristic outbursts. Furthermore, the dataset confirms the confirmation of classical novae occurring in the Magellanic Clouds, as well as recurrent novae occurrences in both the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, respectively. Additionally, our analysis identifies 1,810 novel candidates for lighthouse-type single outburst sources. The dataset processing, storage architecture, and acquisition strategies for these observations are comprehensively detailed in this paper.

This study introduces a novel Trusted Random Number Generator (TRNG) designed to ensure authenticity in randomness production. While most existing TRNG implementations derive entropy from memory cell data, the supply voltage dependency of these components is frequently overlooked. Our research confirms the existence of a high-entropy source within SRAM cells, observable through output variations caused by voltage underscaling. Although SRAM manufacturers guarantee functional correctness only within specific operational ranges, they do not validate TRNG usage for applications requiring certified randomness authenticity. Our novel design leverages the analog characteristics of passing currents through pass transistors, correlating the resulting data differences with voltage variations to generate genuine random outputs. A unique self-calibrating mechanism ensures these outputs remain consistent across diverse nodes, technologies, and storage arrays, with a scaling approach to mitigate potential biases. Validation was conducted across industrial FLASH-enabled workstations and embedded microcontrollers, confirming that TRNR successfully produces authentic randomness on consumer and restricted devices.

This study introduces a modeling methodology for nonvolatile resistive memory devices utilizing small molecular entities as active components. We apply the theory of resistance switching in single-electron tunneling resistors to analyze switching dynamics within single- and double-electron tunneling configurations featuring single or dual dot structures. The work extends to systems comprising three or more dots arranged in series and explores the impact of series dot count on switching characteristics using representative systems based on porphyrin molecules with specific attachment points at the nitrogen or carbon ends. Ultimately, our analysis evaluates the viability of developing large-scale memory systems by integrating nonvolatile resistance switching in molecules governed by single-electron tunneling.

We investigate a fast and slow light scenario within a quadratically q-deformed optomechanical configuration. In this study, we employ the quadrature components of intracavity mechanical and optical fields to demonstrate a clear q-deformation effect on both fast and slow light phenomena. While the observed delays align with previously reported results in standard linear optomechanics, we conclude that using q-deformation provides more precise control over the magnitude and sign of these optical effects.
